ade8684fccda.headline: Man Paints Lady Liberty in 43.5 Seconds, Proving Some People Work Well Under Deadline
body: A man has painted an image of Lady Liberty in just 43.5 seconds, a feat that earned him a Guinness World Records title for the fastest time to paint a landmark statue, according to UPI.

The record was announced as Guinness World Records marked its 22nd GWR Day on Thursday. The annual celebration is traditionally used to unveil new titles and show off record attempts from around the world.

The material available gives few other details. It does not say who the painter is, where the attempt took place, or what style or materials he used, so we will not guess. What we do know is the headline number: under a minute to produce a recognizable portrait of one of the world's most famous monuments.

For perspective, most of us need longer than that to choose a streaming show. The record also shows how Guinness has carved out niche categories, since 'fastest time to paint a landmark statue' is a title that exists only because someone decided to make it one.

GWR Day is a useful reminder that the records business is partly a marketing machine. Each new title generates headlines, social media clips and brand attention for both the record holders and Guinness itself.
ade8684fccda.summary: A man painted Lady Liberty in 43.5 seconds, earning a Guinness World Record for fastest time to paint a landmark statue. The title was announced for the 22nd GWR Day on Thursday.
ade8684fccda.pixel_take: Forty-three and a half seconds for Lady Liberty. Meanwhile, the average office meeting can't even finish agreeing on the agenda in that time.
ade8684fccda.why_it_matters: Record-setting stunts are a durable attention engine, giving brands, creators and Guinness itself free global publicity. Events like GWR Day show how viral-friendly content keeps a long-running media franchise relevant in the social media era.
key_points: A man painted Lady Liberty in 43.5 seconds.
He earned the Guinness record for fastest time to paint a landmark statue.
The title was announced for the 22nd GWR Day on Thursday.

ff4859a231b0.headline: Capita shares crater 70% as chief quits over civil service pension fiasco
body: Shares in UK outsourcing group Capita have lost 70% of their value after chief executive Adolfo Hernandez stepped down with immediate effect, according to BBC News. The exit follows months of delays to payments under the Civil Service Pension Scheme, which Capita has run since December last year.
Hernandez agreed his departure with the board and admitted the company had "not delivered" the service members deserve. Chief financial officer Pablo Andres takes over as acting chief executive.

The scheme covers 1.7 million public sector workers, and tens of thousands of retiring civil servants have faced late payouts. Some people who retired early through ill health have described the wait as "hell", and a Cabinet Office minister called Capita's progress "abysmal" last month. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee, pointed to severe hardship, especially from long-delayed bereavement payments.

The financial damage is stacking up. Capita now expects its 2027 underlying operating profit to take a hit of between £85m and £95m, up from a previous warning of up to £40m. It blames the extra cost of its recovery plan and the loss of two other major contracts in its defence and pension solutions divisions. To shore up its finances, it plans to raise £190m through an equity raise in the first half of next year.

Capita took over from MyCSP in a seven-year contract worth £239m. Russ Mould of AJ Bell said the firm inherited a huge backlog and failed to deliver the automation, AI and digital tools it promised. Government deadlines were missed, milestone payments were withheld and the National Audit Office is probing the contract. Mould said Capita must steady the ship and build on modest recent service improvements.
ff4859a231b0.summary: Capita's shares fell 70% after CEO Adolfo Hernandez quit over delays in the Civil Service Pension Scheme. The firm has cut its profit outlook and plans a £190m equity raise.
ff4859a231b0.why_it_matters: Capita's collapse shows the risk to taxpayers and investors when big public contracts are won on promises of tech-driven efficiency and then fail to deliver. Shareholders face dilution from the planned £190m raise, and the government faces scrutiny over how it outsources essential services.
key_points: Capita shares fell 70% after CEO Adolfo Hernandez left with immediate effect.
The 2027 profit hit is now forecast at £85m-£95m, and a £190m equity raise is planned.
Tens of thousands of civil servants faced pension delays under the 1.7 million-member scheme.

5ab5fd032df0.headline: X Is Building an Undo Button for Accidental Timeline Refreshes, Saving Your Place in the Scroll
body: X appears to be preparing a feature that lets users undo an accidental timeline refresh and return to the exact spot in their feed where they left off, according to Digital Trends. The feature was spotted in a video shared on X by a user named Aaron, and it has not been officially launched.

The problem is familiar to anyone who scrolls. You find an interesting post, and just as you start reading, the feed reloads and replaces it with a fresh batch of updates. Unless you remember who wrote it, finding it again can turn into a small archaeological dig.

The fix is an undo button that appears when the timeline refreshes. Tap it, and you go back to your previous position instead of scrolling through everything again. According to the report, the button stays available for a few seconds, though the exact duration has not been specified.

Digital Trends notes that the change does not reinvent how people use X. It solves a long-standing annoyance that arguably should have existed much earlier. Feeds are built to keep serving fresh content, but that should not come at the cost of whatever you were already reading.

There is no confirmed release date, and it is unclear whether the feature will reach Android, iOS and the web at the same time. For now, it is a preview rather than a promise, so your lost posts will have to keep waiting.
5ab5fd032df0.summary: X is reportedly preparing an undo button that lets users reverse an accidental timeline refresh and return to their previous spot in the feed. No release date or platform rollout has been confirmed.
5ab5fd032df0.pixel_take: Ctrl+Z for your feed: the rare tech update that fixes a problem by giving you back your own time, not by inventing a new way to spend it.
5ab5fd032df0.why_it_matters: Small usability fixes shape how long and how happily people stay in an app, which matters for platforms that depend on attention and advertising. It also shows X focusing on everyday friction rather than big reinventions, a sign of how social platforms compete on polish.
key_points: X is reportedly testing an undo button for accidental timeline refreshes.
The button appears for a few seconds, though the exact time is unspecified.
No release date or platform rollout details have been confirmed.

23de3667e273.headline: Uber pilots 'Recorded Rides,' where your driver's phone camera films the whole trip
body: Uber is piloting a feature in the U.S. called Recorded Rides, which lets passengers book trips in which the driver has turned on the company's Record My Ride tool, according to TechCrunch. The tool uses the front camera of the driver's phone to record the entire drive.
The test is starting in Baltimore, Raleigh, Indianapolis and St. Louis, with more cities planned later. Uber said it is focusing the pilot on rides booked late at night and rides involving teens.
It builds on earlier experiments. Earlier this year Uber introduced live video streaming for rides booked for teenagers, and it has also tested audio recording on late-night trips in some cities.
Uber is also testing automatic recording that would switch on when the app detects a ride going off-course, or when the vehicle may have been in an accident.
Participation is not mandatory. Drivers can opt out of recording through the Settings panel, and riders can decline permission through an in-app notification, the company said.

The pilot shows how ride-hailing platforms are leaning on cameras and sensors to address safety concerns. It also raises the usual questions about privacy, data storage and who can see the footage, none of which were detailed in the material.
23de3667e273.summary: Uber is piloting 'Recorded Rides' in four U.S. cities, letting riders book trips where the driver's phone camera records the drive. Drivers and riders can both opt out.
23de3667e273.pixel_take: Smile, you're on Uber camera. Your 2 a.m. karaoke performance in the back seat may now have a very attentive audience of one lens.
23de3667e273.why_it_matters: Safety is a major factor in ride-hailing trust, and trust drives bookings and revenue. Recording features could reduce disputes and incidents, but they also raise privacy and data questions that regulators and users will watch closely.
key_points: Recorded Rides uses the driver's front phone camera and is piloted in Baltimore, Raleigh, Indianapolis and St. Louis.
Focus is on late-night and teen rides, plus tests of auto-recording for off-course trips or possible accidents.
Drivers can opt out in Settings and riders can decline recording via an in-app notification.

56b22a9072be.headline: Russia Threatens 'Painful Consequences' After Ukrainian Drones Hit Russian Ships in Libya and the Baltic
body: Moscow warned Ukraine on Monday that it will face "painful consequences" for drone attacks on Russian vessels in Libya and the Baltic Sea, according to Al Jazeera. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian Ministry of Defence was handling the response and would release details if it saw fit.

The row follows claims by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that his forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury at a naval base in Benghazi on Sunday and struck a cargo ship he said Russia used to carry weapons. Libya's eastern-based government, a rival to the internationally recognised administration in Tripoli, has complained to the United Nations, saying the strikes violated its sovereignty. It also demanded an international investigation into reports that Ukrainian military personnel were allegedly present in western Libya.

In the Baltic, a drone attack on Saturday set the Kaliningrad-bound Sparta II on fire in international waters. Finland's military said Ukraine likely carried out the strike. Peskov called it a "very dangerous trend" and said it was escalating tensions in the region, adding that Moscow hoped the Baltic states would lean on Kyiv to end what he called "terrorist practices".

The attacks fit a wider Ukrainian push against Russian naval assets and merchant ships tied to the so-called shadow fleet, which helps Moscow get around Western sanctions. Russia's answer on the logistics side was telling: Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said it would spend 47 billion roubles ($576m) on two rail ferries to keep goods moving to Kaliningrad, mostly from the rainy-day fund.

Kaliningrad is an exclave wedged between Lithuania and Poland, and it depends heavily on sea supplies since Lithuania restricted the transit of goods from Russia in line with EU sanctions in 2022. The ferries, running between Ust-Luga and Baltiysk, are not expected to start service until 2030.

Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev, meanwhile, repeated his familiar nuclear rhetoric, writing that Russia has the right to use every means to defend itself, potentially including nuclear weapons. He conceded, though, that Moscow has so far seen no "direct necessity" to do so.
56b22a9072be.summary: Russia vowed "painful consequences" after Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian vessels in Libya and the Baltic. Moscow also announced a 47 billion rouble ferry plan to supply Kaliningrad by sea.
56b22a9072be.why_it_matters: Attacks on shadow fleet and merchant vessels put shipping lanes, insurance costs and sanctions enforcement in the spotlight. Russia's multibillion-rouble ferry plan shows how sea supply risks are forcing real spending from its rainy-day fund.
key_points: Moscow threatens "painful consequences" after Ukrainian drone strikes on ships off Libya and in the Baltic.
Eastern Libya's government complained to the UN over sovereignty violations.
Russia will spend 47 billion roubles ($576m) on Kaliningrad rail ferries due in 2030.

3e33a311aeb0.headline: Tom Lee Says Ether Is Now as Scarce as Bitcoin, and Bitmine Keeps Buying
body: Tom Lee, chairman of Bitmine, argued this week that Ethereum's supply has become about as tight as Bitcoin's, according to Decrypt. The claim came alongside news that Bitmine bought more ETH.

Lee's numbers: ETH's supply has grown just 0.90% annually since mid-2025. Bitcoin's growth over the same stretch is put at 0.82%, so the gap is a sliver, the kind you'd need a magnifying glass and a spreadsheet to spot.

The comparison also stretches to other big networks. Lee said Solana, XRP and Cardano have all expanded their supplies at a much faster pace, which leaves Ethereum looking more like the disciplined sibling of Bitcoin than like its looser smart-contract rivals.

The pitch matters because Bitcoin's appeal has long rested on scarcity, the idea that a fixed, predictable supply protects value over time. If Ethereum can credibly claim similar behavior, it strengthens the case for treating ETH as a store of value, not just fuel for a blockchain.

Of course, the source material here is thin. The teaser does not say how much ETH Bitmine purchased, and the figures are Lee's own framing rather than an independent audit. Also worth remembering: Lee runs a company with a big stake in ETH, so he is hardly a neutral narrator of its virtues.
Still, scarcity arguments tend to move sentiment in crypto, and a corporate buyer adding to its holdings while making that argument is a signal investors will watch closely.
3e33a311aeb0.summary: Bitmine chairman Tom Lee says Ethereum's supply growth of 0.90% a year nearly matches Bitcoin's 0.82% and beats Solana, XRP and Cardano, as Bitmine added more ETH.
3e33a311aeb0.pixel_take: Ethereum is apparently on a strict supply diet, and the chairman of a company that keeps buying it says the results are fantastic. Shocking, a bull with a bag being bullish.
3e33a311aeb0.why_it_matters: Scarcity is a core driver of how investors value crypto assets, so a case that ETH rivals Bitcoin on supply discipline could influence demand. Corporate buyers like Bitmine also show how large holders shape market sentiment, though their claims come with obvious self-interest.
key_points: Tom Lee says ETH supply has grown 0.90% annually since mid-2025, versus Bitcoin's 0.82%.
He says Solana, XRP and Cardano expanded supply far faster.
Bitmine bought more ETH, though the amount was not given in the material.

00eafea95337.headline: Rep. Krishnamoorthi Wants Congress to Make AI Chip Export Rules Permanent, Not Just Policy
body: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi is calling on Congress to write permanent legislative safeguards for exports of advanced AI chips, according to an opinion piece published by The Hill. He argues that the new chip-export rules are a start but should not be left to the whims of any one administration.

The push follows reports of suspected technology diversion, meaning advanced chips that may have ended up somewhere other than their intended destination. The teaser also points to internal disputes within the Trump administration over how such exports should be handled. The material available does not spell out the specifics of those reports or disagreements, so details remain thin.

The core argument is about durability. Export controls set through executive action can be rewritten, loosened or reversed whenever the political winds shift, which makes life hard for both national security planners and the companies that build and sell the chips. A law passed by Congress would be harder to unwind and would give everyone a steadier rulebook.

That logic is familiar in Washington. Rules written by an agency or the White House are quick to adopt but quick to change, while legislation is slow to pass but sticky. Krishnamoorthi is betting that the stakes around advanced AI hardware justify the slower route.

For now this is one lawmaker's call, expressed in a commentary piece, rather than a bill with a vote scheduled. Whether Congress takes it up will depend on how much appetite lawmakers have for locking in chip policy in a fast-moving, politically charged field.
00eafea95337.summary: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi urges Congress to enact permanent safeguards on advanced AI chip exports, citing reports of suspected diversion and internal Trump administration disputes, arguing new rules should outlast any one administration.
00eafea95337.pixel_take: Executive rules on chips are like a sandcastle: lovely, quick to build, and one election tide away from vanishing. Krishnamoorthi would like some concrete, preferably with a congressional stamp.
00eafea95337.why_it_matters: AI chips are among the most valuable and strategically sensitive products in the tech economy, so export rules directly affect chipmakers' sales and market outlook. Permanent law would give companies and investors more predictability than policies that can flip with each administration.
key_points: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi wants Congress to legislate permanent AI chip export safeguards.
The call follows reports of suspected technology diversion and internal administration disputes.
Argument: new rules are a start, but only law makes them durable.

fac080966b18.headline: UnitedHealth, Humana and CVS Slide as Washington Eyes Medicare Advantage Ratings
body: Shares of UnitedHealth, Humana and CVS fell on Monday after reports that the U.S. government is targeting Medicare Advantage ratings, according to MarketWatch. The health insurers are facing scrutiny over their business practices and possible changes to the private Medicare program.

The source material is thin on specifics, so what exactly regulators plan to change remains unclear. What is clear is that investors heard the word 'scrutiny' and reached for the sell button, which is roughly the stock market's version of flinching.

Some background helps. Medicare Advantage is the privately run alternative to traditional government Medicare, and insurers like these three are major players in it. Star ratings, which grade plan quality, are widely understood to influence how much insurers get paid through bonuses and how attractive their plans look to seniors. Any change to how those ratings work can touch revenue and margins.

That is why the market reacts quickly. When a large share of a company's earnings depends on one government-linked program, even a hint of rule changes can shake the share price before the details arrive. Rules that look like fine print in Washington can become a very big number on a balance sheet.

For now, this is a story of uncertainty rather than outcomes. Investors will be watching for official details on what is being targeted, how soon changes could land, and whether the companies respond with guidance or pushback.
fac080966b18.summary: UnitedHealth, Humana and CVS shares dropped as the U.S. government turns its attention to Medicare Advantage ratings, raising fears about scrutiny and possible changes to the private Medicare program, MarketWatch reported.
fac080966b18.pixel_take: Wall Street heard 'scrutiny' and 'ratings' in the same sentence and gave these insurers a rather low score of its own: sell first, read the fine print later.
fac080966b18.why_it_matters: Medicare Advantage is a big profit engine for large health insurers, so policy shifts can quickly move their earnings outlook and share prices. Investors holding health stocks or broad index funds may feel the swings, and seniors in these plans could eventually see changes in coverage.
key_points: UnitedHealth, Humana and CVS shares fell on news of U.S. scrutiny of Medicare Advantage ratings.
Details of the planned changes were not available in the source material.
Ratings can affect insurer payments and plan appeal, making the stocks sensitive to policy shifts.

65237063587f.headline: Python in the Toilet Sparks 48-Hour Search, Turns Out a 9-Year-Old Made It With AI
body: A photo showing a python emerging from a toilet set off a 48-hour search by authorities, only for the image to be revealed as an AI-generated creation made by a 9-year-old, according to UPI.

The details available are thin: the report does not name the child, the location or the authorities involved, so we won't guess at them. What it does make clear is that the picture looked convincing enough to trigger a real search that lasted two days.

The case is a tidy example of how cheap and easy image generation has become. A child can now produce a picture realistic enough that adults act on it, and the effort needed to make something believable has fallen to nearly zero.

For officials, that creates an awkward new routine. A photo used to be at least a starting clue. Now it may be a prank, a homework experiment or a very enthusiastic nine-year-old, and checking takes time and people that could be used elsewhere.

The story ended harmlessly, as far as the report indicates, with the source of the scare identified as AI rather than an actual reptile lurking in the plumbing. Still, it is a reminder to pause before trusting a dramatic image, especially one that shows up without context.
65237063587f.summary: A photo of a python coming out of a toilet triggered a 48-hour search by authorities, until it was revealed as an AI image made by a 9-year-old, UPI reported.
65237063587f.pixel_take: Somewhere a nine-year-old just learned that with the right prompt you can mobilize authorities for two days. Meanwhile adults still can't get a reply to an email.
65237063587f.why_it_matters: Easy AI image tools mean fake visuals can now trigger real-world responses, costing time and public resources. As synthetic images get more convincing, verification becomes a bigger cost for officials, media and businesses alike.
key_points: A python-in-a-toilet photo prompted a 48-hour search by authorities.
The image was AI-generated by a 9-year-old, UPI reported.
The case shows how easily convincing fake images can cause real responses.

7ee65d1ae7eb.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Is Back as CEO Just 11 Days After Resigning Over Affair Scandal
body: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive just 11 days after he resigned amid allegations of two extramarital affairs, according to BBC News. The board said his return is in the best interests of stockholders, employees, partners and customers.

The scandal began on 29 October, when the New York Times reported that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, who is no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman, linked to Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, is a Chinese intelligence asset. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

A second report, about an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who has been at the company for 18 years, prompted a board meeting. Huang's resignation was announced soon after.

He was barely out the door before a 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign appeared, reportedly started by current and former employees, partners, shareholders and supporters. Huang said he would be 'honoured' to return if asked. The board initially showed no interest, then changed course.

The stakes are large. Nvidia dominates the chips that power artificial intelligence and is the world's second most valuable company, according to the BBC. Its customers include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic. The company also sits at the centre of the US-China race for tech leadership.

Huang's personal fortune has swung with the drama. Bloomberg's Billionaires Index put it near $200bn earlier this year, but it has since dropped to around $105bn. His biographer Stephen Witt told the BBC that Huang is a visionary on the level of Steve Jobs, but also described a level of arrogance and self-deception, and noted that Huang worked hard to cultivate a family-man image.
7ee65d1ae7eb.summary: Nvidia's board has brought back Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned over two alleged affairs, one involving a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset.
7ee65d1ae7eb.pixel_take: Eleven days: barely enough time for a leather jacket to go out of style, and a board to discover that firing the AI chip king is bad for business.
7ee65d1ae7eb.why_it_matters: Nvidia's chips underpin the AI boom, so who runs the company matters to markets, partners and anyone with tech stocks in their portfolio. The episode shows how key-person risk and geopolitical sensitivities around China can shake even a giant firm within days.
key_points: Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO 11 days after resigning over two alleged affairs.
US officials allege one woman involved is a Chinese intelligence asset; Huang admitted infidelity and apologised.
His estimated fortune fell from nearly $200bn to about $105bn, per Bloomberg.

264c5cfe8be2.headline: Plaud Note Pro AI Recorder Drops to $149.99, So Your Notes Can Finally Take Themselves
body: Plaud's flagship Note Pro AI note taker is on sale for $149.99 from November 19 through November 30, according to Digital Trends. The 20% cut comes off a usual $189 price, and the deal is available directly from Plaud or on Amazon.

The pitch is simple: software bots can handle Zoom, but they go quiet during phone calls and in-person briefings. The Note Pro is dedicated hardware that attaches magnetically to the back of a smartphone using an included case or ring. It is an aluminum slab about the size of a credit card, 0.12 inches thick and 1.06 ounces, with a 0.95-inch AMOLED screen for checking battery and recording status.

On audio, it combines four microphones with a vibration sensor, offering a 16.4-foot pickup range with AI beamforming and noise suppression. A dual-mode system reportedly detects whether you are on a call or in a room and switches automatically. It has 64GB of storage and up to 30 hours of recording in Enhance mode, or 50 hours in Endurance mode.

The software side matters as much. Plaud Agent turns transcripts, highlights and notes into emails, reports, spreadsheets or presentations, and connects with Google Calendar, Slack, Notion and Linear. Plaud Desktop covers online meetings.
The Starter Plan includes 300 free AI transcription minutes per month. Plaud says it meets SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR and EN 18031 standards and does not train AI models on user data unless people opt in.
As always with limited-time deals, the clock is the catch: the promo ends November 30, and Digital Trends frames it as a rare break on flagship productivity hardware.
264c5cfe8be2.summary: Plaud's flagship Note Pro AI recorder is 20% off at $149.99 through November 30 on Plaud's store and Amazon, down from $189, according to Digital Trends.
264c5cfe8be2.pixel_take: A recorder that listens, transcribes and drafts the follow-up email. Meetings that could have been emails are now emails that write themselves about meetings.
264c5cfe8be2.why_it_matters: AI note-taking is moving from software bots to dedicated hardware, and subscriptions plus a one-time device price shape the real cost. For professionals, a $40 saving is small, but it lowers the entry price of a growing gadget category.
key_points: Note Pro costs $149.99 from Nov 19 to Nov 30, versus $189 usually.
It records calls and in-person talks with four microphones and a vibration sensor.
Starter Plan includes 300 free transcription minutes monthly.

30f1434d7064.headline: Amazon Lists Moto Tag 3 Before Motorola Announces It, and It Looks a Lot Like the Tag 2
body: Motorola's Moto Tag 3 has turned up for sale on Amazon before the company has said a word about it, according to The Verge. The Amazon UK listing has reportedly been live since Friday, just five months after the Moto Tag 2 went on sale in the US.

The listing was spotted by X user @matteventu. It shows the tracker in a "Pantone Lucent White" finish for £24.96 (about $33), with a shipping estimate of one to four months. That is less a delivery window than a season of the year.

Leaker Evan Blass shared a second image showing a purple version, described as "Pantone Indigo Blue" on a separate Amazon Italy listing. Both colors are new: the Moto Tag 2 is currently sold only in orange or a grey-ish beige.

The catch is that the Tag 3 doesn't seem very new. According to The Verge, both trackers use a replaceable CR2032 battery, claim more than 500 days of battery life, and support UWB in Android Find Hub. The model number on the back of the Tag 3 images, XT2561-1, also matches the Tag 2's.

That raises the possibility that the "3" is a labeling slip and these are simply new colors of the Tag 2. Motorola hasn't confirmed either way. The Verge has asked the company for clarification and says it will update the story if it responds.
30f1434d7064.summary: A Moto Tag 3 listing appeared on Amazon UK before any announcement, priced at £24.96. Specs and model number match the Moto Tag 2, so it may just be new colors.
30f1434d7064.pixel_take: Motorola's tracker has already been found by the internet before its own announcement. Irony aside, it may just be the old tag in a fresh Pantone outfit.
30f1434d7064.why_it_matters: Cheap item trackers are a competitive niche, and retailer leaks often reveal product plans before companies do. For shoppers, the episode is a reminder to check specs before paying for a higher version number that may just be a new color.
key_points: Moto Tag 3 appeared on Amazon UK at £24.96 (about $33) before any announcement.
New Pantone colors are the only clear difference from the Moto Tag 2.
Matching battery, UWB support and model number suggest it could be a mislabeled Tag 2.

6a16b32fcddc.headline: Leaked Russian Records Show Over 1,000 Military Suicides in Ukraine War, and Likely Far More
body: More than 1,000 Russian service members have died by suicide since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, according to an analysis by The Guardian of confidential data from Russia's state statistics agency, Rosstat. The figures come from a leaked cache of more than 11m death certificates.

The Guardian identified 1,087 suicides among military personnel. At least 614 occurred in occupied parts of Ukraine or in Russian border regions, mainly Belgorod and Bryansk. A further 885 deaths in or near Ukraine were logged as firearm injuries of "undetermined intent", a category experts say can hide suicides. Together, the suicides add up to roughly a regiment of dead.

The records show a steady climb: more than 50 in 2022, more than 200 in 2024, a peak of 365 in 2025, and almost 300 already in 2026 despite incomplete records. Of the suicides in the war zone, 43 involved soldiers aged 18 or 19. The data also includes 108 men under 25 who died away from the front, some probably conscripts pressed into signing contracts that allow deployment.

Analysts say the true toll is higher. Ivan Chuvilyaev of Idite Lesom, a group that helps soldiers desert, called the numbers a low estimate and said reports are simply passed up the chain. He and military analyst Rob Lee noted that soldiers who kill themselves on the battlefield, for example when wounded or as a drone approaches, would likely be recorded as combat deaths.

The Guardian cited cases where families were told one thing and records showed another. Lt Col Sergei Savenok's wife was told his death was suicide, yet his certificate lists an undetermined firearm injury. Private Alexander Lazor's family was told he died in combat, but two comrades said their unit was told he took his own life.

Lee pointed to coercion, abuse and fear of dangerous missions inside the Russian army. The Kremlin does not publish military suicide data and treats casualty figures as a state secret. Mediazona reported 20,662 men facing military court cases for refusing to serve by the end of May 2025, and IStories found at least 49,000 servicemen declared deserters or absent without leave.
6a16b32fcddc.summary: Leaked Rosstat data analysed by The Guardian records over 1,000 suicides among Russian military personnel since the invasion of Ukraine, with experts saying the real figure is almost certainly higher.
6a16b32fcddc.why_it_matters: The data offers a rare window into morale and losses inside Russia's army, which the Kremlin treats as secret. Hidden strain on manpower and discipline matters for how long Russia can sustain the war, and for sanctions, energy and market risk tied to it.
key_points: Guardian found 1,087 military suicides in leaked Rosstat data, plus 885 "undetermined intent" firearm deaths near Ukraine.
Recorded suicides rose from over 50 in 2022 to 365 in 2025, with almost 300 already in 2026.
Experts and activists say the real toll is higher because many cases are likely recorded as combat deaths.

0c873259805e.headline: Quantum computers could one day come for $72 billion in ETH, researchers warn, and they have a fix
body: Researchers say Ethereum wallets holding roughly $72 billion worth of ether could be exposed to a future quantum attack, according to a CoinDesk report published on November 23, 2026. The at-risk accounts are those whose public keys are visible on the blockchain.

According to the findings, these accounts hold nearly 55% of all ether that is not locked up in staking. That makes the issue less an obscure corner case and more a question about where most of the network's liquid wealth is sitting.

The concern rests on a well-known idea in cryptography: a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could, in theory, work backward from a visible public key to the private key that controls the funds. Accounts that have exposed their public keys give a would-be attacker a head start. No such machine is described in the material as existing today, so this is a warning about the future rather than a live theft.

The researchers did not stop at the alarm bell. They propose a way to migrate these accounts to quantum-resistant security, which would let holders move to newer protections before the threat becomes practical. The teaser does not detail how the proposal works, so the specifics remain to be seen.

The story highlights a broader challenge for crypto: blockchains are built to be hard to change, yet security assumptions can age. Upgrading a network with this much value at stake takes coordination among developers, wallet providers and ordinary holders, and that kind of herding is famously slower than any quantum processor.
0c873259805e.summary: Researchers say Ethereum accounts with visible public keys hold about $72 billion in ETH, nearly 55% of non-staked supply, and could be vulnerable to future quantum attacks. They propose migrating to quantum-resistant security.
0c873259805e.pixel_take: Quantum computers may someday crack wallets like piñatas, so the researchers are suggesting we swap the candy for a vault first. Getting everyone to actually move, though, is the real puzzle.
0c873259805e.why_it_matters: Nearly 55% of non-staked ether sits in accounts that could be targeted if quantum computing advances, so the issue touches the security assumptions behind a huge pool of value. Investors and developers will be watching whether a migration plan gains traction well before any real threat arrives.
key_points: Accounts with visible public keys hold about $72 billion in ETH.
They represent nearly 55% of ether outside staking.
Researchers propose moving them to quantum-resistant security.

aaf0595a93ae.headline: Carney shares a stage with Trump and Carney impersonators at Ottawa press dinner
body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney took the stage on Saturday at the annual Parliamentary Press Gallery dinner in Ottawa alongside two impersonators: one playing himself and one playing U.S. President Donald Trump, according to The Hill.

The Hill's report says Carney announced he was "pressing the…" before the teaser cuts off, and the full text of the remark was not available to us. The headline's "Fake news" line is a nod to the evening's comedic tone, though the material does not say who delivered it or in what context.

The Press Gallery dinner is a long-running tradition in which politicians and journalists set aside their usual sparring for an evening of roasting each other. Self-deprecating humor from the guest of honor is part of the script, and bringing along a double of yourself and of the leader of your largest trading partner is a fairly bold way to follow it.

The pitch is simple: instead of selling coins and possibly triggering a tax bill, a holder pledges them as collateral and borrows against them. It is the crypto version of taking out a loan on your house rather than selling the kitchen.

The material available does not specify details such as interest rates, loan-to-value ratios, liquidation terms or when the product becomes available. Those are the things borrowers should check first, because the fine print decides whether this is a handy tool or an expensive surprise.

Crypto-backed lending is not new, but it has a mixed history. Earlier waves of lenders in the sector ran into trouble, which is part of why a bank with a regulated footprint offering such loans through a established consumer lending channel draws attention.

Still, the story as reported is narrow: a bank, a partner, and a loan range. Whether it signals a broader move by traditional lenders toward digital assets as collateral will depend on how the product performs and how many other banks follow.

ce3073bd5d64.headline: Russian strikes kill at least 15 in Kyiv region as Ukraine hits Russian oil sites and ships
body: Russian strikes on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people overnight into Monday, according to Ukrainian officials, with rescuers still searching rubble for survivors after a block of flats partially collapsed in the town of Dymer, about 45km north of the capital.

Regional official Tymur Tkachenko said at least 11 people died in the five-storey building in Dymer. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said the dead included a teenager and that 11 people, among them two children, could not be reached. Rescuers have pulled out survivors, including a 79-year-old woman and a child.

Elsewhere, a strike on a supermarket in Vyshneve, just south of Kyiv, killed three people and wounded 15, including three children, Mayor Illya Dikov said. One more person died in Bila Tserkva when a private home was hit and caught fire. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

The attacks come days after Vladimir Putin promised a "much more painful" response to Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge. Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the section used by vehicles and halting train services, according to Al Jazeera. Moscow has also stepped up pressure on Ukraine's energy network as temperatures fall toward freezing.

Ukraine kept up its own campaign. Drones hit oil storage facilities in Russia's Tatarstan region, about 1,000km from the Ukrainian border, along with a petroleum products plant in Rostov and reportedly the city of Perm, home to a large refinery. Russian news agency Interfax reported fires but no immediate casualties.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. He said a second target, the cargo ship MV Angara, was hit, and that a Ka-27 helicopter was destroyed. These claims come from Zelenskyy and were not independently verified in the material.
ce3073bd5d64.summary: Russian strikes killed at least 15 people in the Kyiv region, mostly in a collapsed apartment block in Dymer. Ukraine reported hitting Russian oil facilities and, per Zelenskyy, sinking a Russian corvette.
ce3073bd5d64.why_it_matters: Attacks on energy infrastructure on both sides feed into oil and power supply risks as winter approaches. Strikes on Russian refineries and storage sites can affect fuel supply and keep energy markets sensitive to the war's escalation.
key_points: At least 15 killed in Kyiv region, including 11 in a collapsed block of flats in Dymer.
Strikes follow Putin's pledge of a 'much more painful' response over Kerch Bridge attacks.
Ukraine hit Russian oil facilities and says it sank a Russian corvette near Libya.

f205e38d2cf7.headline: Marvel's final Avengers: Doomsday trailer packs in nearly every hero, and Doom wants their 'stolen lives' back
body: Marvel has released the final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday, after days of rumors, according to Ars Technica. The film, the penultimate chapter of the MCU's Phase Six and a milestone for the so-called Multiverse Saga, opens in theaters on December 18, 2026.

The footage suggests the Avengers will pay for tampering with the timeline to undo the blip in Endgame. Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom tells the assembled heroes that all of them have lived stolen lives, and that they must now give them back.

The story is set 14 months after Thunderbolts*. The official logline promises heroes from three universes on a deadly collision course: Earth-616 (the Avengers, Wakandans and New Avengers), Earth-828 (the Fantastic Four) and the original X-Men. The cast list includes Chris Hemsworth, Anthony Mackie, Pedro Pascal, Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen and many more, with cameos expected from the likes of Tom Holland and Benedict Cumberbatch.

Chris Evans' Steve Rogers gets a big role. The trailer opens with him and Peggy Carter agreeing they made the right choice, though Steve feels guilty about keeping the truth from their teenage son. We also learn that the couple built their life in the same alternate universe as the Fantastic Four, who show up to recruit him. Most of the rest is previously seen footage, plus new moments such as Cyclops facing Doom and several Sentinels, and Thor grumbling that he doesn't know who half the group is.

Wanda Maximoff doesn't appear, though she may be among three Latverian witches who briefly show up. Ars Technica says it's unclear whether the film will match Infinity War and Endgame, but it should be a spectacle.
The release date sets up a box-office showdown: Dune: Part III opens the same day. Avengers: Secret Wars, due December 17, 2027, will close out Phase Six.
f205e38d2cf7.summary: Marvel's final Avengers: Doomsday trailer crams in heroes from three universes and hints Doctor Doom blames the Avengers for 'stolen lives.' The film opens December 18, 2026, against Dune: Part III.
f205e38d2cf7.pixel_take: Marvel's casting strategy appears to be 'yes.' Thor admits he doesn't know half the team, which makes him the audience, and also the person who needs a spreadsheet.
f205e38d2cf7.why_it_matters: Big franchise tentpoles move studio fortunes and theater traffic, and a head-to-head opening against Dune: Part III makes this a closely watched box-office clash. Guinness World Records has long welcomed quirky twists on ordinary activities, and this one fits the pattern: take a familiar motion, add an awkward handicap, and see how far human determination can stretch. UPI published video of the feat.

c2ee55235eac.headline: ECB Preps to Take Tokenized Securities as Collateral, Targeting June 2027
body: The European Central Bank plans to let banks pledge more tokenized securities as collateral, according to Cointelegraph. The aim is to start accepting securities issued on platforms licensed under the EU's distributed ledger pilot program in June 2027.

In plain terms, collateral is the stuff banks hand over to the central bank in exchange for funding. Until now, that pile has mostly consisted of traditional assets sitting in traditional systems. The ECB's plan would widen the door to securities that are born and recorded on blockchain-style infrastructure, as long as they come from platforms that hold a license under the EU pilot regime.

That license condition matters. The plan does not appear to be a free-for-all for any digital token with a ticker and a dream. It points only to securities issued on venues that regulators have already approved under the distributed ledger pilot program, which is designed as a controlled testing ground for this technology.

The source material gives only the headline and the target date, so details such as eligibility criteria, haircuts or which specific platforms might qualify are not available here. The June 2027 timing is described as an aim, not a done deal, so the schedule could still shift.

Even so, the direction is clear: a major central bank is signaling that tokenized assets can be part of the plumbing of regular monetary operations, not just a side experiment. For banks and market infrastructure firms building on distributed ledgers, that is a meaningful vote of confidence.
c2ee55235eac.summary: The ECB aims to begin accepting securities issued on platforms licensed under the EU's distributed ledger pilot as collateral in June 2027, according to Cointelegraph, widening the role of tokenized assets.
c2ee55235eac.pixel_take: The ECB is telling tokenized securities they can finally sit at the grown-ups' table, provided they show a license at the door and wait until June 2027.
c2ee55235eac.why_it_matters: Central bank acceptance makes tokenized securities more useful, since assets that can be pledged for funding are more attractive to hold and issue. It could encourage banks and platforms to invest in blockchain-based market infrastructure across Europe.
key_points: The ECB aims to accept more tokenized securities as collateral starting June 2027.
Eligible securities would be issued on platforms licensed under the EU's distributed ledger pilot program.
Details like criteria and haircuts were not included in the available material.

4f474af5544e.headline: Alienware's 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor drops to $280, its lowest price yet
body: Alienware's AW2726DM, a 27-inch QD-OLED gaming monitor, is on sale for $279.99 at Best Buy and Dell ahead of Black Friday, according to The Verge. That is $70 below its original $349.99 price and the lowest it has been so far.

The panel runs at 1440p resolution with a 240Hz refresh rate. The Verge's reviewer bought one at launch and has used it for both work and play for several months, calling it a monitor that looks and performs like one costing hundreds more.

The appeal comes from the QD-OLED technology. It delivers strong contrast, deep blacks and fine control over brightness, things that cheaper panel types struggle to match. The 240Hz refresh rate also gives a graphics card plenty of room to push fast frames in PC games, and the monitor works well with consoles too.

Connectivity is covered by HDMI and DisplayPort inputs. The one notable flaw the reviewer points to is the lack of USB-C video support, which could matter if you want to connect a laptop with a single cable.

According to the reviewer, the monitor still holds up against newer models and had more features than similarly priced rivals at launch. The Verge suggests it as a holiday gift for yourself or the gamer in your life. As the outlet notes, it may earn a commission on purchases made through its links.
4f474af5544e.summary: Alienware's 27-inch 1440p 240Hz QD-OLED AW2726DM is $279.99 at Best Buy and Dell, down from $349.99, according to The Verge. It is the monitor's lowest price yet.
4f474af5544e.pixel_take: OLED contrast used to cost a small fortune. Now it costs less than many wallets expect on Black Friday, and the only thing missing is USB-C video.
4f474af5544e.why_it_matters: OLED gaming monitors have long carried a hefty premium, and a sub-$300 QD-OLED shows how fast that premium is shrinking. For shoppers, holiday sales on last-generation hardware can deliver the best value per dollar.
key_points: The AW2726DM is $279.99 at Best Buy and Dell, down $70 from $349.99.
It is a 27-inch 1440p QD-OLED panel with a 240Hz refresh rate.
Its main flaw is the lack of USB-C video support.

48ebf8f03916.headline: Report Says Gaza Is a 'Toxic Wasteland', With Contamination Across 99% of Its Territory
body: A new study says Israel's war has left toxic contamination across 99% of Gaza's territory, according to Al Jazeera's report on the findings. The pollution includes heavy metals, explosive residues and biological hazards.

The report warns that these contaminants threaten the health of Palestinians and the local environment for decades. The material available does not give details on how the study was conducted or who carried it out, so those points remain unclear.

Heavy metals and explosive residues are the kind of pollutants that do not simply disappear once the fighting stops. They can linger in soil and water, and can enter the food chain. Biological hazards, which typically come from damaged sanitation and unburied waste, add a separate public health risk.

The scale of the figure, 99% of the territory, suggests that contamination is not confined to a few hot spots. Any future cleanup would therefore have to be vast, and that matters for planning reconstruction.

Environmental remediation of this kind is expensive and slow, and it usually requires specialist equipment, expertise and long-term funding. Those needs will weigh on any plan for rebuilding housing, farmland, water systems and other infrastructure in Gaza.
This article is based on a summary of the report's headline findings. Further detail on methods, specific pollutants and recommendations was not available in the material reviewed.
48ebf8f03916.summary: A new report says toxic contamination, including heavy metals, explosive residues and biological hazards, covers 99% of Gaza, threatening health and the environment for decades, according to Al Jazeera.
48ebf8f03916.why_it_matters: Contamination on this scale could add major cost and delay to any reconstruction of Gaza, since land and water would need cleanup before rebuilding. It also raises long-term health burdens and questions about who will fund remediation.
key_points: A new study finds toxic contamination across 99% of Gaza's territory.
Pollutants include heavy metals, explosive residues and biological hazards.
The report warns of health and environmental threats lasting decades.

Flanagan also spoke about the incoming group of new senators, describing the class as diverse in lived experience and in geography, according to The Hill's teaser. The full context of her comments was not available, so it is unclear which specific policies or officials she had in mind.

The framing is a familiar one in politics: the idea that Washington is out of touch with kitchen-table concerns while the rest of the country is dealing with the consequences. Newly elected lawmakers often use that contrast to signal they plan to shake things up, and to set themselves apart from the institution they are about to join.

Whether the rhetoric turns into action is the open question. A freshman senator has limited power on her own, and the Senate's rules and narrow margins tend to slow even popular ideas. Still, the comments offer an early look at the tone Flanagan intends to bring to the chamber.
5d73a5474c02.summary: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) said Sunday that the federal government isn't effectively addressing everyday Americans' problems, arguing people outside Washington know things are 'on fire,' according to The Hill.

A date on a calendar is a promise, not a product, and launches in this sector have a long record of shifting.

For readers weighing anything connected to the project, the sensible approach is to wait for primary documents such as official announcements, technical documentation and any independent audits before drawing conclusions. Until then, December 18 is simply a date to watch.
