Employees left more than 1,600 comments urging reinstatement on an internal suggestion post, and a public petition has passed 200,000 signatures, mostly from self-identified shareholders. Elon Musk and Garry Tan said they signed or planned to. Trump had said he "would not mind" Huang's return.

The stakes are large. Nvidia held about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026 and was the first company valued above $4 trillion, though its stock has fallen sharply since Huang resigned. Huang said he returns with "the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
8425a12bb072.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after his resignation over alleged affairs, reversing its earlier stance after employee, shareholder and White House pressure.
8425a12bb072.pixel_take: The board's 'we do not intend to' lasted about as long as a gadget's launch-day battery. Turns out a 200,000-signature petition and a falling stock price make excellent mediators.
8425a12bb072.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of AI infrastructure, so who runs it affects chip supply, investor sentiment and portfolios heavy in tech. The episode also shows how governance, politics and US-China export concerns can sway a trillion-dollar company's decisions.
key_points: Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO 11 days after resigning on November 12.
The board reversed its November 17 stance after employee, shareholder and government input, including from Trump.
Nvidia's stock has fallen sharply since the resignation; it held about 90% of the GPU market as of September 2026.

6def2ae63f11.headline: Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang After Reported Call From Trump, Stock Surges
body: Nvidia announced on Monday that Jensen Huang is returning as CEO, hours after Semafor reported that President Donald Trump personally joined a board meeting to argue for his reinstatement. According to an opinion column in The Hill, the shares jumped roughly 30 percent that day.

The board had initially decided Huang should go. The Hill's columnist, Aron Solomon, notes that allegations against him include affairs with employees, among them a reported relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. The piece does not say how those claims were resolved, only that the board reversed course.

Solomon's argument is not about whether Huang deserves the job. He says that is Nvidia's business. His concern is the president speaking up in a boardroom for a specific executive at a publicly traded company, and what that does to directors' independence.

He is careful on the facts: Trump's advocacy does not prove he pressured anyone or changed any votes, and the board may have been heading that way already. He also grants that the White House has a legitimate interest in any national security question, since Nvidia's chips sit at the center of the global race in AI and advanced computing.

The column draws a line between sharing a view and entering the debate over who holds the top job. It asks readers to imagine the shoe on the other foot: a future president urging a board to oust a CEO who criticizes the administration, or to keep one who is politically loyal.

Solomon also points out that presidents have long clashed with industry, citing Kennedy and the steel companies and the government's role in the auto sector during the 2008 crisis. He says boards owe fiduciary duties to shareholders, not to pleasing the president, and should be ready to explain the reversal to them.
6def2ae63f11.summary: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO after Semafor reported Trump joined a board meeting to back him. A Hill column says the stock jumped about 30 percent and questions the president's role.
6def2ae63f11.pixel_take: Nvidia's board reportedly got a surprise guest on the call. Usually the only outside voice in a boardroom is a consultant billing by the hour; this one apparently came with a bigger title.
6def2ae63f11.why_it_matters: Nvidia's value rides on AI chips, so who runs it moves markets, as a roughly 30 percent single-day jump shows. If political pressure can sway boardroom decisions, investors face a new kind of governance risk that is hard to price.
key_points: Semafor reported Trump called into Nvidia's board meeting to argue for Huang's return.
Nvidia shares rose about 30 percent on the day, per The Hill column.
The column says the issue is board independence, not whether Huang deserves the job.

d1baf1523e99.headline: Falklands oil plans stir fears for seals, whales and penguins
body: The Falkland Islands, whose oil reserves are claimed in a long-running sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the UK, are at the center of a new environmental debate, according to The Guardian. Environmentalists worry that drilling plans could threaten one of the richest ecosystems in the Atlantic.

The Guardian's report, published on November 23, 2026, describes the main islands as two large, jagged shapes set against the South Atlantic. The teaser points to a wildlife-rich region of seals, whales and penguins, which is why conservation groups are watching the oil ambitions closely.

The headline quote, 'Once installed, there's no getting rid of it', captures the core worry: oil infrastructure, once built, tends to stay for decades. The full text of the article was not available to us, so details of specific projects, companies and timelines are not covered here.

The backdrop is a familiar one. Argentina and the UK each dispute the other's claim over the islands and the resources around them, so any oil development carries diplomatic weight as well as ecological risk. Offshore energy projects are rarely only about energy.

For the wider economy, the story is a reminder of the trade-off facing many resource-rich regions: potential revenue and investment on one side, fragile ecosystems and long-term liabilities on the other. Add a sovereignty row, and the risks for investors and governments multiply.
d1baf1523e99.summary: The Guardian reports that environmentalists fear Falklands oil plans could harm seals, whales and penguins, as Argentina and the UK continue to dispute sovereignty over the islands and their reserves.
d1baf1523e99.why_it_matters: Offshore oil projects in disputed waters mix energy economics, geopolitics and environmental risk. Investors and governments must weigh potential revenue against long-term liabilities and diplomatic friction, which can affect project costs and timelines.
key_points: Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the Falklands and its oil reserves.
Environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic's richest ecosystems, including seals, whales and penguins.
Critics warn that oil infrastructure, once installed, is hard to remove.

39c640fb84a1.headline: Spain's IBEX 35 Closes Up 1.71% as Madrid Markets Finish in the Green
body: Spanish stocks ended the session higher on Monday, November 23, 2026, with the benchmark IBEX 35 index gaining 1.71% at the close of trade in Madrid, according to Investing.com.

That is a solid daily move for a blue-chip index. A gain of nearly two percent in one session is the kind of day that makes investors check their portfolios twice, just to make sure the numbers are real.

The source report gives only the headline figure. It does not say which companies or sectors drove the rally, what the index level was at the close, or what prompted the buying. Without those details, it would be guesswork to pin the move on any single cause.

For context, the IBEX 35 tracks the 35 most liquid stocks on Spain's exchanges and is heavily weighted toward banks, energy and utilities, and large multinational firms. Because of that mix, the index often reacts to shifts in interest-rate expectations, global risk appetite and broader European market sentiment.
One strong session does not make a trend. Investors will be watching whether the momentum carries into the coming days or whether Monday proves to be a one-day bounce.
39c640fb84a1.summary: Spain's IBEX 35 rose 1.71% at the close on November 23, 2026, according to Investing.com. The report gave no details on what drove the gain.
39c640fb84a1.pixel_take: A 1.71% jump is the stock market's version of a good espresso: no explanation needed, just a noticeable lift. Whether it lasts past Tuesday is another story.
39c640fb84a1.why_it_matters: The IBEX 35 is a key gauge of Spanish and wider European equity sentiment, so a sizable daily gain can signal improving risk appetite. For anyone holding European funds or Spanish stocks, it is a welcome move, though one day alone says little about direction.
key_points: The IBEX 35 rose 1.71% at the close on November 23, 2026.
Spanish stocks finished higher, per Investing.com.
The report did not name the drivers of the rally.

663bd019eb60.headline: Polish Stuntman Zips Nearly 570 Feet While Fully on Fire, Because Why Not
body: A professional stuntman from Poland has traversed a zip line stretching 568 feet and 6.8 inches while his entire body was on fire, according to UPI. The feat was shared as a video under the outlet's Freak News coverage.

The details available are thin: the report gives the distance and the fact that the stuntman was fully ablaze, but the material provided does not name the performer, the location, or any record claim. We will not guess at what we were not told.

What we can say is that the distance is roughly the length of one and a half American football fields, a long way to travel as a human torch. Most of us feel brave after sending an email without proofreading it.

Full-body-burn stunts are a known niche in the stunt world and are normally carried out by trained professionals with specialized preparation and safety teams. Nothing in the source says what precautions were used here, so viewers should treat this as a spectacle to watch, never to imitate.

As for the economics, stunts like this tend to live off viral attention. A clip that travels the internet can raise a performer's profile and bookings, which is a very modern way of turning a very hot idea into a career.
663bd019eb60.summary: A professional stuntman from Poland rode a zip line for 568 feet and 6.8 inches with his entire body on fire, UPI reported. Video of the stunt was shared online.
663bd019eb60.pixel_take: Most people's morning commute feels like it's on fire. This stuntman made it literal and added a zip line, which is at least a more efficient route.
663bd019eb60.why_it_matters: Viral stunts show how attention has become a currency: a single striking video can lift a performer's profile and earning power. It is also a reminder that extreme feats carry real risks and rely on professional expertise.
key_points: A Polish professional stuntman zip lined 568 feet and 6.8 inches.
His entire body was on fire during the ride, per UPI.
The report did not name him or give location or safety details.

ad1e59530bc5.headline: How to pair Bluetooth headphones with Windows 11, and what to do when it misbehaves
body: Pairing Bluetooth headphones with a Windows 11 PC is meant to be easy, but it can still be fiddly, according to a new how-to guide from Engadget published in late November 2026. The good news: there are a few reliable routes, and if yours fails, you are probably not the problem.

The quickest method starts at the taskbar. Click the speaker icon in the bottom-right corner to open quick settings, then click the arrow beside the Bluetooth icon and make sure Bluetooth is switched on. Next, put your headphones or earbuds into pairing mode. How that works varies by product, but it usually means holding a button, often one marked with the Bluetooth logo. When your device shows up in the list, select it and you are connected.

You can also go through Settings. Press Win + I, choose Bluetooth & devices from the left-hand menu and confirm the Bluetooth toggle is on. For a first-time pairing, click Add device, then Bluetooth, and make sure your headphones are in pairing mode. The PC scans for nearby gear, and once your device appears, click it and wait a few moments.

A third option is Swift Pair, which tries to do the pairing proactively. Engadget notes that popular headphones such as the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, along with earlier models in those lines, support it. With Bluetooth enabled on the PC, turn on the device and enter pairing mode. A pop-up should ask whether you want to connect; click Connect. Devices paired this way will connect automatically in future.

Then comes the awkward part. Engadget says Bluetooth performance has long been a weak spot for Windows 11, and Microsoft was still working to improve it as of September 2026. If pairing fails, the guide suggests updating your wireless drivers or simply rebooting the PC before blaming yourself or your headphones.
ad1e59530bc5.summary: Engadget walks through three ways to pair Bluetooth headphones with Windows 11: quick settings, the Settings app and Swift Pair. It also warns that flaky Bluetooth is a known Windows weak spot.
ad1e59530bc5.pixel_take: Three ways to pair your headphones, and one reliable fallback: turn the PC off and on again and hope Bluetooth is feeling generous.
ad1e59530bc5.why_it_matters: Wireless headphones are now the default for many people, so a smooth connection to a work or gaming PC affects everyday productivity. Knowing the fixes can also save a trip to the store or a needless replacement purchase when the real culprit is a driver.
key_points: Pair via the taskbar quick settings or Win + I, then Bluetooth & devices.
Swift Pair offers a pop-up connection and auto-reconnects on supported headphones.
Windows 11 Bluetooth is still shaky; try driver updates or a reboot if pairing fails.

620631940a36.headline: Bitcoin Bounces Back to $61K After a Weekend Roller Coaster to a Two-Year Low
body: Bitcoin clawed its way back to about $61,000 after a wild weekend in which it hit a two-year low, according to Decrypt. The price swung by more than $6,000 over the period, the kind of move that makes a casual glance at your portfolio feel like a jump scare.

The sell-off did not happen in isolation. Decrypt reports that tech stocks slid over the same stretch, a reminder that Bitcoin often trades less like digital gold and more like a risk asset that catches a cold whenever equities sneeze.

Adding to the gloom, spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded their largest single-day outflow since June, per the report. These funds let investors get exposure to Bitcoin through ordinary brokerage accounts, so heavy withdrawals suggest that some of the more traditional money was heading for the exits as prices fell.

The rebound to $61K offers some relief, but the source material does not say what drove the recovery or whether it can hold. A bounce after a sharp drop is common in volatile markets, and it does not by itself signal that the worst is over.
For now, the takeaway is simple: the move was big, fast and tied to broader market jitters. Anyone holding crypto, directly or through an ETF, got a vivid lesson in how quickly sentiment can swing.
620631940a36.summary: Bitcoin recovered to around $61,000 after hitting a two-year low over the weekend, swinging more than $6,000 as tech stocks fell and spot ETFs saw their biggest daily outflow since June, Decrypt reports.
620631940a36.pixel_take: Bitcoin spent the weekend doing a $6,000 limbo dance, then popped back up like nothing happened. Your stomach, sadly, is still somewhere near the two-year low.
620631940a36.why_it_matters: Bitcoin's link to falling tech stocks shows it still behaves like a risk asset, not a safe haven. ETF outflows matter because they show how mainstream investors react under stress. If you hold crypto, expect big swings and size positions accordingly.
key_points: Bitcoin hit a two-year low over the weekend, then rebounded to about $61K.
The price swung by more than $6,000 as tech stocks slid.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw their biggest daily outflow since June.

90f831b4fd3e.headline: Nvidia Brings Jensen Huang Back as CEO Less Than Two Weeks After His Resignation
body: Nvidia's board announced on Monday that it has reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned. According to TechCrunch, he stepped down after admitting to at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy.

The board said it consulted senior government officials before concluding that Huang posed no national security risk. It described its decision as unanimous and said it was satisfied with Huang's candor and ability to lead after a series of meetings and discussions with him.
Investors cheered. Shares jumped in premarket trading and opened about 30% higher. At 9:51 a.m. ET they were priced at $159.95, up 27%.

President Donald Trump publicly backed the move on Truth Social, saying the board made the correct decision. He also said the attorney general had confirmed the government has no evidence Huang engaged in illegal activity. A group of tech executives, including Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney and Garry Tan, signed a petition urging reinstatement.

The U-turn is sharp. Days earlier, board chair Harvey C. Jones said on the third-quarter earnings call that the board did not plan to bring Huang back, and Nvidia had hired Heidrick & Struggles to search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, served as interim CEO and keeps her finance duties.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, said he returns with humility and renewed commitment, and that he can't wait to get back to work.
90f831b4fd3e.summary: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO under two weeks after he resigned over admitted affairs. Shares surged about 30% as the board cited consultations with government officials.
90f831b4fd3e.pixel_take: Nvidia's CEO search lasted about as long as a software update that gets cancelled halfway: lots of progress bars, then everyone shrugged and restored the old version.
90f831b4fd3e.why_it_matters: Nvidia is the world's most valuable chipmaker and central to the AI boom, so leadership swings move markets and index-heavy portfolios. The episode also shows how tightly chip companies are tied to national security politics and government views.
key_points: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and president after his resignation less than two weeks earlier.
Shares opened roughly 30% higher after the announcement.
The board said it consulted senior government officials and found no national security risk.

a8d519390506.headline: Don Toliver Manchester Concert Evacuated After 'Unknown Substance' Affects Crowd
body: A concert by American rapper Don Toliver in Manchester was evacuated on Sunday after people in the crowd began experiencing effects from what was described as an unknown substance, according to The New York Times.

The reported symptoms prompted an emergency response. The material available so far does not say what the substance was, how many people were affected, or how serious their condition was, so those details remain unclear.

Evacuations at live events are a standard precaution when something potentially hazardous appears in a packed space. Venues and emergency services generally prioritise getting people out first and identifying the cause afterward, which is why early reports are often thin on specifics.
Further information is expected to come from authorities and the venue. Until then, it is best to treat the cause as unconfirmed and avoid speculation about what was released or how it got there.

For the live music business, incidents like this are a reminder of how much of the industry runs on crowd safety planning. Large concerts depend on security, medical teams and clear evacuation procedures, and the costs of getting any of them wrong are far higher than the price of a ticket.
a8d519390506.summary: A Don Toliver concert in Manchester was evacuated Sunday after audience members were affected by an unknown substance, prompting an emergency response, according to The New York Times. Details remain scarce.
a8d519390506.why_it_matters: Safety incidents at large events can lead to cancellations, refunds, insurance claims and tighter security rules, which affect promoters, venues and ticket buyers. The live entertainment sector depends on public confidence that crowds are safe.
key_points: Don Toliver's Manchester concert was evacuated on Sunday.
Crowd members experienced effects from an unknown substance, prompting an emergency response.
The substance, number of people affected and their condition have not been detailed.

57fa941fb53d.headline: US Lands 2031 Women's World Cup Matches, Joining Mexico and Others in Hosting Lineup
body: The United States has been chosen as a host site for the 2031 Women's World Cup, according to The Hill. The announcement comes after this summer's men's tournament, which the outlet says brought millions of international travelers to the country.

The Hill also reports that the men's event earned FIFA the most profitable World Cup in its history. That track record likely helped the case for handing the US another turn on the global stage, though the teaser does not spell out how the decision was made.

The US will not be going it alone. The teaser says Mexico will take part along with Costa, and the text cuts off there, so the full list of co-hosts is not available in the material we have. We will not guess at the rest of the roster.

The bigger picture is straightforward: big tournaments are big business. Visitors book flights, hotels and restaurant tables, broadcasters pay for rights, and sponsors line up. A hosting slot five years out gives cities, businesses and investors a long runway to plan.
Details such as specific cities, stadiums and match schedules were not included in the material, so those questions remain open for now.
57fa941fb53d.summary: The US will host Women's World Cup matches in 2031, with Mexico and others, after a men's tournament that The Hill says was FIFA's most profitable ever.
57fa941fb53d.pixel_take: The men's tournament just left the building and the US is already booking the sequel. Hotels, take note: the trophy tour never really ends.
57fa941fb53d.why_it_matters: Major tournaments move real money through travel, hospitality, media and sponsorship. A confirmed 2031 slot gives host-area businesses and investors years to plan. It also signals how lucrative FIFA's events have become.
key_points: The US will host Women's World Cup matches in 2031.
Mexico is among the co-hosts, per The Hill.
This summer's men's Cup reportedly was FIFA's most profitable ever.

202f9d858fca.headline: South East Water swings to £22.9m loss after a summer of dry taps and costly clean-up
body: South East Water has reported a pre-tax loss of £22.9m for the six months to 30 September, a sharp turnaround from the £18.2m profit it posted in the same period a year earlier, according to BBC News. The company serves about 2.4 million customers across south-east England.

The hit comes from penalties and the cost of dealing with supply disruption over the summer. The company said it spent £29m responding to interruptions during heatwaves in Kent and Sussex, including bottled water, emergency water stations and customer compensation. It has also set aside £14.6m in its latest results to cover a redress package.

The regulator Ofwat had already stepped in. In July it ordered the company to spend £30.5m on improvements after outages affected more than 286,000 customers across Kent and Sussex. The firm supplies water to Kent, East and West Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire, and hosepipe bans remain in force across all its areas.

The finances have been shaky for some time. In October the company had to ask shareholders for £50m, after warning earlier in the year that it needed extra funding to stay afloat. Leadership has also been reshuffled: John Halsall became chief executive after former chief executive David Hinton and chair Chris Train stepped down, following MPs saying they had no confidence in the leadership. Richard Morse is due to become chair on 3 December, succeeding interim chair Lisa Clement.

South East Water said it sees early signs of improvement and plans a significant transformation of the business, though it warned customers will take time to notice. A spokesperson said customers will judge the firm on whether supply is more reliable, communication is better and support is right, and promised evidence in future results.
202f9d858fca.summary: South East Water posted a £22.9m half-year pre-tax loss, versus an £18.2m profit a year earlier, after summer supply failures, penalties and £29m of response costs. A leadership overhaul is under way.
202f9d858fca.why_it_matters: Utility failures can quickly turn a profit into a loss through penalties, compensation and emergency spending, and they put pressure on shareholders to inject cash. For customers, the story is about reliability, bans on water use and how regulators enforce standards on essential services.
key_points: Pre-tax loss of £22.9m in six months to 30 September, against an £18.2m profit a year earlier.
Costs included £29m on summer disruption response and £14.6m set aside for redress.
Company asked shareholders for £50m in October and is changing its leadership.

77b00f318ebd.headline: Portugal's PSI Edges Up 0.39% as Lisbon Closes the Day in the Green
body: Portugal's stock market finished higher on Monday, with the benchmark PSI index gaining 0.39% at the close of trade in Lisbon, according to Investing.com.

That is the extent of the detail available. The report, dated November 23, 2026, does not say which companies led the advance or lagged, how many stocks rose versus fell, or what trading volumes looked like. So any story about why the market moved would be guesswork, and we would rather not make things up.

What can be said is that a 0.39% gain is a modest, ordinary-sized move. It is the sort of session that rarely sets off alarms or champagne corks, more a polite nod from investors than a standing ovation.

For context, the PSI is Portugal's main stock index, tracking a group of the country's largest listed companies. Because it is a small market by European standards, it is usually watched as a gauge of local sentiment and as one piece of the wider European picture, rather than as a global market mover.

Daily moves like this one are best read as a snapshot, not a trend. One green day says little about where the market is heading, and investors typically look at weeks and months of data, along with company earnings and economic news, before drawing conclusions.
77b00f318ebd.summary: Portugal's PSI index rose 0.39% at the close of trade on Monday, according to Investing.com. No details on drivers or individual stocks were available.
77b00f318ebd.pixel_take: A 0.39% gain: the stock market equivalent of a polite nod across the office. Nobody's popping champagne, but nobody's crying into their spreadsheet either.
77b00f318ebd.why_it_matters: Daily index moves help investors gauge the mood in a market, even if one small gain says little on its own. For anyone holding European or Portuguese equities, it is a reminder to focus on longer trends rather than single sessions.
key_points: Portugal's PSI index rose 0.39% at the close, per Investing.com.
No information was provided on which stocks drove the move.
A single modest daily gain is a snapshot, not a trend.

952f98d917c3.headline: Nvidia Soars 33% After Huang's Return, Adding $36 Billion to His Fortune and Torching Short Sellers
body: Nvidia shares jumped more than 33% after the company's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang 11 days after his resignation, according to Decrypt. The surge added over $36 billion to Huang's personal fortune.
Short sellers, who bet that a stock will fall, took the brunt of the move. Decrypt reports they lost about $12 billion in a single day, their worst one-day loss since at least 2019.

The material provided does not explain why Huang resigned or why the board brought him back, so those details remain unclear. What the numbers do show is how much investors tie Nvidia's value to its leader.

Short squeezes work in a simple, painful way. When a stock rockets higher, short sellers must buy shares to close their positions and cap their losses. That buying can push the price up even further, turning a bad day into a worse one.

A 33% one-day gain is extraordinary for a company of Nvidia's scale, and it shows how sensitive the market is to leadership news at firms central to the technology boom. For Huang, whose wealth is largely tied to his Nvidia stake, a swing of this size is mostly paper gains that can move just as fast in the other direction.
952f98d917c3.summary: Nvidia stock leapt over 33% after the board reinstated Jensen Huang 11 days after his resignation, adding more than $36 billion to his wealth and costing short sellers about $12 billion, per Decrypt.
952f98d917c3.pixel_take: Eleven days away and the market threw him a welcome-back party. Short sellers, meanwhile, were the guests who got handed the bill and a very long receipt.
952f98d917c3.why_it_matters: It shows how much a single executive can move the value of a market-leading tech company, and how fast leveraged bearish bets can unravel. Anyone holding Nvidia directly or through index funds felt the swing, and short squeezes like this are a reminder of the risks of betting against momentum.
key_points: Nvidia shares rose more than 33% after Jensen Huang was reinstated 11 days after resigning.
Huang's wealth rose by over $36 billion, according to Decrypt.
Short sellers lost about $12 billion, their worst single-day loss since at least 2019.

93e285e5c9b2.headline: Zelensky says Ukrainian drones hit Russian ships off Libya, as Kremlin warns of rising tensions
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has posted footage on social media that he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday, according to BBC News. It would mark a striking extension of the war far from Ukraine's borders.

Zelensky said Ukrainian drones sank a Russian warship and that the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship he said was being used to transport weapons. The material does not name either ship.

The BBC said it verified footage showing a ship ablaze at the port of Benghazi. That confirms a fire at the scene, but it does not by itself establish who carried out the attack or which vessel was hit.

Libya's local health ministry said it received injured people from a commercial ship targeted off the coast. It is unclear whether that is the same vessel Ukraine says it attacked, so key details remain unconfirmed, including the casualty picture.
The Kremlin responded by warning of an escalation of tensions in the region, but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

If Ukraine's account holds, the strikes would show its drone campaign reaching well beyond the Black Sea. Shipping through the Mediterranean is a vital artery for global trade, and any attack near busy ports tends to make insurers, shipowners and governments nervous. For now, the claims come largely from one side, and independent verification is limited to the fire in Benghazi.
93e285e5c9b2.summary: Zelensky says Ukrainian drones sank a Russian warship and hit a weapons-carrying cargo ship off Libya. The BBC verified footage of a burning ship at Benghazi; the Kremlin warned of escalating tensions.
93e285e5c9b2.why_it_matters: Attacks on shipping far from the Black Sea can raise risk perceptions for Mediterranean trade routes, which can feed into insurance costs and freight rates. Investors also watch whether the war widens geographically, since that tends to affect energy and commodity sentiment.
key_points: Zelensky says drones sank a Russian warship and targeted a weapons-carrying cargo ship off Libya.
The BBC verified footage of a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port, but it is unclear if it is the same vessel.
The Kremlin warned of escalating regional tensions without directly commenting on the attacks.

2f73cb50563e.headline: Virginia and Oregon Take SpaceX to Court Over AI Deepfake Porn and CSAM Allegations
body: The attorneys general of Virginia and Oregon announced separate lawsuits against SpaceX on Monday, according to The Hill. The suits accuse the company of creating and promoting AI-generated deepfake pornography and child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

Virginia's complaint, per the outlet's report, accuses SpaceX of failing to prevent the harmful content. The teaser does not spell out the rest of the allegations, and the full text of the filings was not available for this report, so further details about the claims remain unclear.
The two states filed their cases separately rather than jointly. That means each will proceed under its own state's laws and courts, and each attorney general can pursue its own remedies.

The case adds to a growing pile of legal and regulatory scrutiny of generative AI. Lawmakers and prosecutors in the US and abroad have been pressing companies to show that their image tools cannot be used to produce sexualized fakes, especially anything involving minors. CSAM is illegal regardless of whether it is photographed or synthesized, and state officials have signaled they will use existing consumer protection and criminal-adjacent statutes to go after it.

SpaceX has not been quoted in the material provided, so its response to the allegations is not known here. Allegations in a lawsuit are claims, not findings, and it will take time for the courts to test them.
2f73cb50563e.summary: Virginia and Oregon's attorneys general filed separate lawsuits against SpaceX, accusing it of creating and promoting AI deepfake pornography and child sexual abuse material, The Hill reports.
2f73cb50563e.why_it_matters: State-level lawsuits over AI-generated explicit content could set legal precedents that raise compliance costs and liability risk for any company building or deploying generative AI. Investors and users should watch how courts treat responsibility for AI outputs.
key_points: Virginia and Oregon announced separate lawsuits against SpaceX on Monday.
The suits allege creation and promotion of AI deepfake porn and CSAM.
Virginia's suit also accuses SpaceX of failing to prevent the content.

2d44b1976e56.headline: Child safety groups tell Amazon and eBay: pull AI toys until they're proved safe
body: More than 150 child safety groups and experts spanning six continents have urged Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI-powered toys this Christmas until they can be shown to be safe, according to The Guardian.

The advocates say they are worried about privacy and about the possibility that the toys communicate with children in inappropriate ways. The material available does not name specific products or companies beyond the two retailers being targeted.

The call lands at the busiest point of the shopping calendar, when online marketplaces move enormous volumes of toys and gadgets. Putting the pressure on Amazon and eBay makes strategic sense: they are gatekeepers that many parents rely on, and a policy change from them would reach far more households than a campaign aimed at any single toy maker.

The concerns fit a wider pattern. Toys that connect to the internet and talk back can collect data, including children's voices and habits, and generative AI can produce unpredictable replies. A teddy bear that improvises is charming in theory, but a product that cannot be fully controlled is a harder sell when its audience is small children.

Neither retailer's response is included in the material available, so it is unclear whether either company plans to act. For now, the demand is for a pause until safety is demonstrated, not a permanent ban.
2d44b1976e56.summary: More than 150 child safety groups and experts across six continents want Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys this Christmas until they're proved safe, citing privacy and inappropriate communication concerns.
2d44b1976e56.pixel_take: Nothing says holiday magic like a toy that chats back, and a coalition of 150 groups would like proof it won't say anything weird first.
2d44b1976e56.why_it_matters: Marketplaces face growing pressure to vet connected, AI-driven products, which could mean tighter listing rules and compliance costs for toy makers. For parents, it is a reminder that a smart toy can bring data and privacy trade-offs along with the fun.
key_points: More than 150 groups and experts across six continents signed the appeal.
They want Amazon and eBay to halt AI toy sales this Christmas until safety is proved.
Concerns include privacy and inappropriate communication with children.

96b4ccbec80e.headline: Dutch Stocks Have a Great Monday as the AEX Climbs 2.15%
body: Netherlands stocks closed higher on Monday, November 23, 2026, with the AEX index gaining 2.15% by the end of trading, according to Investing.com.

That is a hefty move for a benchmark that usually prefers to stroll rather than sprint. A gain above 2% in a single session is the kind of day that makes a trader glance at the screen twice and then quietly pretend they expected it.

The material available gives only the headline figure. It does not say which companies drove the rise, what news triggered it, or how other European markets performed the same day. Without that detail, any explanation of the cause would be guesswork, and we would rather not make things up.

What can be said is general context. The AEX tracks the largest companies listed on the Amsterdam exchange, so a broad rise of this size usually reflects strength across several heavyweight stocks rather than a quirk in one name. Big single-day moves can come from economic data, central bank expectations, corporate results or shifts in global sentiment, though the source does not say which applied here.

For investors, one strong day is a data point, not a trend. Markets often give back gains as quickly as they win them, so the next sessions will show whether Monday was the start of something or just a very pleasant afternoon.
96b4ccbec80e.summary: The Dutch AEX index closed up 2.15% on Monday, November 23, 2026, according to Investing.com. The source gives no explanation for the rally.
96b4ccbec80e.pixel_take: The AEX didn't just rise, it hit the gym. Whether it's a new routine or a one-day pump, we'll know by Tuesday's weigh-in.
96b4ccbec80e.why_it_matters: A 2%-plus daily jump in a major national index can shift sentiment and affect the value of pension funds and index investments tied to Dutch and European stocks. One day alone doesn't set a trend, but it is worth watching for follow-through.
key_points: The AEX closed up 2.15% on November 23, 2026.
Reported by Investing.com, with no cause or company details given.
A single strong session does not confirm a lasting trend.

48c4e1713bfe.headline: GrapheneOS Builds Its Own RCS App, Though Google Still Gets a Plus-One
body: GrapheneOS, the privacy-focused Android-based operating system for Pixel phones, has built a proof-of-concept RCS messaging app that works without Google Messages, according to Digital Trends. There is no release date yet.

Today, GrapheneOS users who want RCS must install Google Messages and turn on sandboxed Google Play. The new prototype removes the first requirement. It still leans on sandboxed Play services for things like phone number verification, so the breakup with Google is more of a trial separation.

The prototype uses end-to-end encryption through Messaging Layer Security (MLS), and GrapheneOS says it is compatible with Google Messages and iOS. It supports typing indicators, delivery and read receipts, reactions, and photo and file sharing. An official demo shows an encrypted chat between a Pixel 7 Pro and a Pixel 9.

The developers plan to fold what they learn into GrapheneOS's built-in messaging app rather than ship a separate one. Before a public release, the app needs SMS and MMS fallback, since the prototype currently handles RCS only.

The longer-term goal is a fully standalone option for carriers that support RCS independently of Google. That is a hurdle, because most carriers still use Google's RCS infrastructure and require a token from Google Play.
GrapheneOS also says the app is not meant to replace a dedicated secure messenger, and strict privacy purists may well stay with apps like Signal.
48c4e1713bfe.summary: GrapheneOS has built a proof-of-concept encrypted RCS app that works without Google Messages and is compatible with Google Messages and iOS. It still needs sandboxed Google Play at first and has no release date.
48c4e1713bfe.pixel_take: GrapheneOS is dumping Google Messages but keeping Google Play in the contacts, sandboxed, at arm's length. It's the most polite way to say 'it's complicated.'
48c4e1713bfe.why_it_matters: RCS is becoming the default texting standard between Android and iPhone, and it mostly runs through Google's infrastructure. Efforts like this show how hard it is to get modern messaging without depending on a big platform. For privacy-minded users, fewer required Google apps means more control over their data.
key_points: GrapheneOS built a proof-of-concept RCS app with MLS encryption, compatible with Google Messages and iOS.
The first version still needs sandboxed Google Play for verification but not Google Messages.
SMS and MMS fallback is still missing and there is no release date.

4aa00cdbe5eb.headline: French police call in a shaman to exorcise their station's 'evil spirits' after staffing woes
body: Police officers at the Lourdes Police Station in France reportedly brought in a shaman on October 31 to rid the building of 'evil spirits', according to Metro, which cites reporting by the French satirical paper Le Canard Enchaîné.

The ceremony was said to be aimed at 'cleansing' the station after complaints about staff shortages and stressful working conditions. The idea reportedly came from an officer who felt the place needed to be cleared of negative energy. The ritual was meant to 'cleanse the memory of the place'.
Police union representative Rémi Gonzalez told the broadcaster Ici Béarn-Bigorre that the station commander simply wanted to find a way to relieve his teams.

Local authorities were less than enchanted. The prefecture confirmed the visit was a 'personal initiative by the officers' and said it was paid for with their own money. It stressed that senior police officials had not ordered the ceremony.
In a statement to BFMTV, the prefecture said the prefect interviewed the hierarchical leaders as soon as the facts became known.

For context, a shaman is a spiritual practitioner who enters altered states of consciousness to interact with the spirit world for healing. Whether the station feels any lighter has not been reported, though the underlying complaints about staffing and stress appear to remain on the books.
4aa00cdbe5eb.summary: Officers at France's Lourdes Police Station reportedly hired a shaman to cleanse the building of 'evil spirits' amid staffing and stress complaints. The prefecture says officers paid themselves and questioned leaders.
4aa00cdbe5eb.pixel_take: When the rota can't be fixed, call the spirits. Cheaper than hiring more officers, though apparently the paperwork demons are still on shift.
4aa00cdbe5eb.why_it_matters: The episode shows how understaffing and workplace stress in public services can push staff toward unconventional fixes. Real solutions cost public money for hiring and support, and strained services affect the quality of public safety that taxpayers fund.
key_points: A shaman reportedly performed a cleansing at the Lourdes Police Station on October 31.
Officers cited staff shortages and stressful conditions; they paid for it themselves.
The prefecture called it a personal initiative and questioned station leaders.

e1f23138583f.headline: Grocers Eat the Cost of Thanksgiving Bundles to Lure Shoppers, and Smaller Chains Feel It Most
body: Grocery chains are selling Thanksgiving meal bundles at prices that cost them money, hoping the deals will pull shoppers through the door, according to The New York Times. The squeeze is landing hardest on smaller grocers.

The logic is classic loss-leader retailing: sell a headline item cheaply and count on shoppers to fill their carts with other things. A discounted holiday meal bundle is a very visible way to say 'we're the affordable option' at the busiest food-shopping moment of the year.

But the Times reports that the math works differently depending on who is doing it. Giants like Walmart may still profit from these deals because of their sheer size, which gives them buying power and room to absorb thin margins on some products.

Smaller grocery chains don't have that cushion. When they match big-box prices on the centerpiece items of the holiday table, they can end up genuinely out of pocket, and they have less scale to make it back elsewhere in the store.

For shoppers, that means a good deal on the turkey-and-trimmings front. For the industry, it is another reminder that price competition tends to favor the biggest players, and that a holiday promotion can be a bargain for customers while being a headache for the retailer offering it.
e1f23138583f.summary: Grocers are selling Thanksgiving meal bundles at a loss to attract shoppers. Giants like Walmart may still profit thanks to scale, while smaller chains are feeling the squeeze, the New York Times reports.
e1f23138583f.pixel_take: Thanksgiving's real main course is margin pressure: giants carve the turkey comfortably, while smaller grocers are left with the drumsticks and the bill.
e1f23138583f.why_it_matters: Holiday discounting shows how scale shapes who can win a price war in food retail. Shoppers may save on their feast, but sustained losses could pressure smaller grocers and, over time, reduce competition and choice.
key_points: Grocers are selling Thanksgiving meal bundles at a loss to draw shoppers.
Walmart and other large retailers may still profit because of their size.
Smaller grocery chains are feeling the squeeze from the deals.

d3d91d3fb456.headline: Paolo Bulgari, Italian Jewelry Heir Who Steered Sale to LVMH, Dies at 89
body: Paolo Bulgari, a member of the Italian jewelry dynasty bearing his name, has died at 89, according to The New York Times. He served as chairman of the family company and was known for a bold, maximalist aesthetic that drew on the look of ancient Rome.

The Times reports that after the 2008 financial crisis, Mr. Bulgari steered the sale of the business to LVMH. That deal moved a family-run name into the orbit of one of the world's largest luxury groups.
The source material available to us is brief, so details about his career, the terms of the sale and the circumstances of his death are not covered here.

Even so, the outline is clear. Bulgari built its identity on richness and historical drama rather than restraint, an approach that set it apart in a field where many houses lean on understated elegance. Mr. Bulgari was among the figures who carried that vision through the company's years as a family enterprise.

His role in the LVMH sale also reflects a wider pattern in luxury. Independent family houses have often joined large conglomerates, which bring scale, distribution and financial muscle, while the brand name and heritage remain the main assets.
d3d91d3fb456.summary: Paolo Bulgari, chairman of the Italian jewelry family's company and champion of Rome-inspired maximalism, has died at 89. He steered the post-2008 sale of the business to LVMH, the NYT reports.
d3d91d3fb456.why_it_matters: The sale of Bulgari to LVMH shows how family-owned luxury houses can end up inside global conglomerates, especially after a financial shock. For investors and consumers, it highlights how heritage brands become scalable assets.
key_points: Paolo Bulgari, chairman of the family jewelry company, died at 89.
He championed a maximalist style that recalled ancient Rome.
After the 2008 financial crisis he steered the sale of the business to LVMH.

7cad82252131.headline: Tesla's FSD v15 makes your commute look like Grand Theft Auto, and regulators are watching
body: Tesla has started rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, which it calls a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system, according to The Verge. The update began reaching cars on Saturday and centers on a new feature called Reality View.

Reality View replaces the old blocky wireframe graphics with a real-time, generative, overhead camera view of buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians and nearby traffic. Drivers can tap the screen to influence what the car plans to do next. The look drew instant comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI, and Elon Musk posted on X that "FSD is GTA irl."

Under the hood, v15 uses an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla's FSD, Robotaxi and Optimus humanoid robot programs. Tesla says it trained the model on millions of online videos and that it now prevents serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power. That figure is Tesla's own claim. The update targets AI4 (HW4) vehicles and upcoming Cybercab platforms, so millions of older HW3 cars are left out.

There are practical additions too. Bike Rack Mode lets drivers use FSD with hitch accessories attached, though reversing, Summon and Autopark are disabled. The car can ease off speed near traffic cameras, with an option to mute specific cameras after two cancellations. Tesla also promises better handling of potholes, standing water and small animals, smoother driving in school zones and bad weather, and navigation that learns favorite routes and parking spots. The cabin camera can now track driver attention through hats and sunglasses, with fewer alerts at higher speeds.

The timing is awkward. NHTSA is investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of running red lights, improperly crossing railroad tracks and driving into oncoming lanes. Dozens of fatalities have been linked to Tesla's driver-assistance systems since 2019. The system still legally requires a human watching the road, and a video-game-style screen may be either a useful window into the car's logic or a fresh distraction. Tesla offers a map-only option and a quieter mode for those who find it too much.
7cad82252131.summary: Tesla is rolling out FSD v15 with a photorealistic Reality View display and a claimed 25x safety gain. Older HW3 cars are excluded, and NHTSA is still investigating about 2.9 million FSD vehicles.
7cad82252131.pixel_take: Tesla made the dashboard look like a blockbuster game, which is bold for a system that still needs a human to keep their eyes on the actual road, not the cutscene.
7cad82252131.why_it_matters: Tesla's valuation leans heavily on its autonomy story, so claims like a 25x safety gain and regulatory outcomes can move the stock and the robotaxi timeline. For owners, the hardware cutoff means older HW3 cars miss the upgrade, which affects resale value and trust in past FSD purchases.
key_points: FSD v15 adds Reality View, a photorealistic real-time overhead display
Tesla claims 25x fewer serious mistakes; it is built for HW4 and Cybercab, leaving HW3 behind
NHTSA is investigating about 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles

f556e1423256.headline: Bitcoin's Rebound Runs Out of Puff as Nvidia and the AI Trade Steal the Spotlight
body: Bitcoin's recent bounce is already fading, according to CoinDesk, as investors pile back into artificial intelligence stocks while the largest cryptocurrency lags behind. Traders cited by the outlet said persistent selling from U.S. investors continues to weigh on bitcoin.

The contrast is stark. Nvidia has jumped more than 30% and has recovered most of the losses it suffered since CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, per the same report. In other words, the AI trade has come back with a bang, while crypto is still hunting for its second wind.

The material available does not spell out the details behind the U.S. selling, so it is hard to say who exactly is offloading coins or why. What traders did make clear is that the pressure has not gone away, and that it is holding back bitcoin even as risk appetite elsewhere returns.

The story shows how competitive the market for investor attention can be. When money rotates toward a hot theme such as AI, assets that once shared the same risk-on enthusiasm can be left behind. Bitcoin and big tech have often been treated as cousins in sentiment, but this week they are behaving more like distant relatives who only meet at weddings.

For readers, the takeaway is that a bounce is not the same as a trend reversal. A rally that fizzles quickly can signal thin demand, and with a rival trade soaking up enthusiasm, bitcoin may need a fresh catalyst of its own to regain momentum.
f556e1423256.summary: Bitcoin's rebound is losing steam as U.S. selling persists, CoinDesk reports, while Nvidia has surged more than 30% and recovered most of its losses since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO.
f556e1423256.pixel_take: Bitcoin showed up to the rally and found the AI crowd already holding the good seats. Nvidia is sprinting; bitcoin is still tying its shoes.
f556e1423256.why_it_matters: Money rotating into AI stocks can pull attention and capital away from crypto, shaping how bitcoin trades in the near term. For anyone holding either, it is a reminder that short bounces can fade fast and that sentiment shifts between themes quickly.
key_points: Bitcoin's rebound is already losing steam, per CoinDesk.
Nvidia has jumped more than 30%, recovering most losses since Jensen Huang stepped down.
Traders say persistent U.S. selling is holding bitcoin back.

540d07d0d868.headline: Florida City Cancels Its Christmas Parade, Blaming a Property Tax Overhaul
body: Deltona, Florida, has cancelled its Christmas parade, with city officials pointing to the state's voter-approved Amendment 3 property tax overhaul, according to The Guardian. The decision comes as the city tries to keep its finances in order.

The teaser describes the move as a response to pending state legislation tied to the amendment, and says the goal is to ensure the city remains on solid financial footing. The original article text was not available to us, so details such as the parade's cost, the size of the expected budget gap and what else may be cut are not known.

The story is a small, festive-shaped example of a familiar pattern. When voters approve limits or reductions on property taxes, local governments, which rely heavily on those revenues to pay for services, often start looking for places to trim before the bill arrives. Big-ticket items like policing and road repair are politically painful to touch, so smaller, visible events can be the first to go.

That visibility is the point. A cancelled parade is something residents notice immediately, which makes it a handy way to show that tax changes have real local consequences. Whether it is a genuine budget necessity or also a bit of political theater is something the available material does not settle.
For now, the takeaway is simple: Amendment 3 has not even fully arrived, and Deltona is already skipping the floats.
540d07d0d868.summary: Deltona, Florida, has cancelled its Christmas parade, citing Florida's voter-approved Amendment 3 property tax overhaul and pending state legislation, as the city moves to protect its finances, The Guardian reports.
540d07d0d868.pixel_take: Property tax reform hasn't even landed yet and it has already cancelled Christmas. Somewhere, a budget office is humming 'Bah, humbug' in four-part harmony.

Wireless terminals that can be set up quickly let units move and communicate with less preparation.

7f3845c3cd12.headline: Compass Group Reportedly Set to Trade Its London Home for Wall Street, Leaving the LSE with a Smaller Lunch Table
body: Catering giant Compass Group is planning to move its primary stock market listing from London to the United States, according to a source close to the company who spoke to the BBC. An official announcement is expected alongside its full-year results on Tuesday. The move was first reported by the Financial Times.

The reason, it is understood, comes down to where the customers and the investors are. North America accounts for two-thirds of Compass's business, which pushed total 2025 revenues to $46.1bn. The company runs brands such as Levy, Bon Appétit, Eurest, Morrison Healthcare and Chartwells, feeding people at stadiums, schools, universities, visitor attractions and offices. It calls itself "possibly the biggest business you've never heard of".

For the London Stock Exchange, it is another unwelcome departure. Arm Holdings, Just Eat, Deliveroo and Paddy Power's parent company Flutter have all left in recent years, and speculation continues over the futures of Shell and AstraZeneca, which began listing shares in New York in February.

There is some reassurance for UK staff. The proposed shift is understood to have no impact on the number of UK employees, and Compass is expected to keep a secondary listing in London. A consultation with investors could take more than a year. There was a hint of what was coming: in April, Compass switched the currency of its standard shares on the LSE from sterling to US dollars.

The LSE's chief, Dame Julia Hoggett, has urged the government to make the UK more attractive for investment and to create structural incentives to back British companies. The scale gap is stark: last year London saw 23 IPOs raising £2.1bn, while the US had 354 raising $44bn (£33bn).
7f3845c3cd12.summary: Compass Group is reportedly planning to make the US its primary listing venue, with an announcement expected Tuesday. It adds to a string of firms leaving London for deeper American markets.
7f3845c3cd12.pixel_take: London's stock market keeps getting stood up by blue-chip dates who say they're just moving where the money is. Compass feeds 600,000 staff, yet the LSE is the one going hungry.
7f3845c3cd12.why_it_matters: Each major company that shifts its main listing reduces liquidity and prestige in London, and may weaken the UK's case as a place to raise capital. For savers and pension funds, a thinner home market can mean fewer domestic investment choices and less influence over how firms are run.
key_points: Compass Group is expected to announce a move of its primary listing from London to the US on Tuesday.
North America makes up two-thirds of its business, with 2025 revenues of $46.1bn.
A secondary London listing is expected and UK jobs are understood to be unaffected.

3254ef278d69.headline: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble 14 hours after Russian strike on Ukrainian village of Dymer
body: A seven-year-old boy was rescued alive from the ruins of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, about 14 hours after a Russian strike hit the village, Ukrainian officials said. The overnight attack on Sunday killed 11 people, according to BBC News.

The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. Regional head Tymur Tkachenko said a 79-year-old woman was also pulled out alive and is being treated in hospital. Authorities said the boy is in stable condition and was taken to hospital.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 130 people are working at the scene and will continue until they have complete information about every person. He said the strike practically blew a section of the building apart, and that rescue work is being complicated by constant new air raid alerts. Earlier, Tkachenko said six people were injured and others were still missing.

Dymer was not the only target. Tkachenko said a strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one person and set the building on fire. Zelensky said a separate strike on a grocery store in Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, killed three people and wounded 13. Mayor Illya Dikov said three children were among the injured.
Vyhivskyi said more than 70 strikes hit 10 Ukrainian regions by Sunday evening. Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said Russia also hit a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
3254ef278d69.summary: A seven-year-old boy was rescued alive 14 hours after a Russian strike on Dymer near Kyiv killed 11 people. Further strikes hit other towns across Ukraine, officials said.
3254ef278d69.why_it_matters: Continued strikes on homes, shops and power infrastructure deepen the human and economic toll of the war, adding to reconstruction costs and risks to energy supply. Such attacks also keep pressure on markets and policymakers watching the conflict and its effect on aid and sanctions.
key_points: A 7-year-old boy and a 79-year-old woman were rescued alive from the rubble in Dymer.
The Dymer strike killed 11 people; more strikes hit Bila Tserkva and Vyshneve.
Over 70 strikes hit 10 regions, and a power substation was also targeted, officials said.

ade7fd04f3e8.headline: Bitcoin Finally Clears Yesterday's High, Ending a Record Run of Lower Highs
body: Bitcoin climbed above the previous day's peak on Sunday, according to CoinDesk, breaking a record streak of consecutive 'lower highs.' The move is being read as an early hint that selling pressure may be easing.

A lower high simply means that each day's top price is below the one before it. String enough of those together and you get a staircase pointing down, which is how technical analysts often describe a persistent downtrend. Sunday's move snapped that pattern, at least for a day.
Before anyone pops confetti, the bigger picture is still rough. The teaser notes that bitcoin remains down 21% in November, so this is a small step up after a long slide, not a victory lap.

Traders pay attention to this kind of signal because it suggests buyers are willing to pay more than the market's recent peak. One higher high does not make a trend reversal, though. Analysts usually look for follow-through, such as more higher highs and higher lows, before calling a bottom.

The original article text was not available, so details such as exact price levels, trading volumes or analyst commentary are not covered here. What is clear is the headline fact: the downward streak of daily peaks is over, and the market now has to show whether Sunday was a turning point or just a pause.

09afcc847896.headline: Nvidia Board Does a U-Turn and Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Brief Exit
body: Nvidia announced on Monday morning that its board has voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, President and board director, reversing course just days after saying he would not be coming back, according to The Verge.

The board said it reached its decision after a series of discussions with Huang, which left it satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead." It also said it consulted "senior levels of the United States government" and concluded his return poses no national security risk. Donald Trump praised the move on Truth Social and said the Attorney General had confirmed the government has no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang.

The backstory is messy. Huang resigned earlier this month after reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and with two Nvidia employees, one of them an executive who reported to him. The board's investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot will continue, with his cooperation.

The reversal is abrupt. Board chair Harvey Jones said on an earnings call last week that the board "does not intend" to bring Huang back. Meanwhile, more than 200,000 people, including Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, Garry Tan and Travis Kalanick, signed a letter urging his return. Nvidia shares fell during his absence, and analysts worried about an outsider taking over at a pivotal moment for the AI boom.

On the leadership chart, interim CEO Colette Kress stays on as CFO and Jones remains the recently appointed board chair. Huang said he is honored to return and approaches the job with "the greatest humility and renewed commitment."
09afcc847896.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO days after saying it wouldn't, citing talks with him and input from U.S. officials. The probe into a reported Chinese spy plot continues.
09afcc847896.pixel_take: Nvidia's board went from "he's not coming back" to "welcome back" in about a week. Corporate governance, now with the pacing of a streaming series and a 200,000-signature petition.
09afcc847896.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, so who runs it moves markets and investor confidence. The shares fell in Huang's absence, and the swift reversal shows how much the company's value is tied to one leader. Government involvement also signals how closely chips and national security are linked.
key_points: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, President and director.
The board said U.S. government input showed no national security risk; its probe into the reported spy plot continues.

The story fits a familiar pattern in personal finance coverage. c3c44e55bd12.headline: Belgium Grinds to a Halt as Unions Strike Over Austerity and a Wobbling Government
body: Belgium came to a near standstill on Monday as trade unions staged a national strike against the federal government's austerity plans, cancelling hundreds of flights and trains, according to Al Jazeera.

Air traffic controller Skeyes said it could not provide regular services, so Brussels airport announced that all departing and arriving flights between 7am and 9pm local time would be cancelled. Charleroi airport, used by low-cost carriers such as Ryanair, also saw air traffic halted. Buses, schools and other public services were disrupted as well.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which speaks for about 25 carriers, said this was the 11th strike to affect Belgian airspace in as many months. That is less a one-off protest than a recurring calendar entry.

Behind the walkout is a budget fight. The government of Prime Minister Bart De Wever wants to save 10 billion euros ($10.9bn) in the coming years to shrink a high deficit. Options under discussion include spending cuts, notably in healthcare, and a VAT increase. Unions want taxes on high earners to offset some of the cuts.

The plan is also dividing the ruling coalition. De Wever has already offered King Philippe his resignation, but the monarch refused it and gave him more time to find a way out. After another week of talks ended without a deal, the prime minister set a new deadline of December 31. His office said that without a budget agreement by then, the government would effectively be unable to govern, ending its existence.

Belgium is not alone. Al Jazeera notes that protests over living costs are continuing across Europe, as governments try to balance stretched public finances against households squeezed by rising prices.
c3c44e55bd12.summary: A national strike over austerity cancelled hundreds of flights and trains across Belgium, while Prime Minister Bart De Wever faces a December 31 deadline to agree a budget or see his government effectively end.
c3c44e55bd12.pixel_take: Eleven airspace strikes in eleven months: Belgium's most reliable public service may now be the walkout. Meanwhile the government has until New Year's Eve to balance a budget, which is a tough party trick.
c3c44e55bd12.why_it_matters: Repeated strikes hit travel, business logistics and consumer confidence, and a budget stalemate can unsettle investors watching Europe's deficits. The outcome, whether VAT rises or high earners are taxed, will directly affect what Belgians pay and receive from public services.
key_points: Hundreds of flights and trains were cancelled, and Brussels airport scrapped all flights from 7am to 9pm.
The government seeks to save 10 billion euros, with healthcare cuts and a VAT rise under discussion.
De Wever set a December 31 budget deadline after the king refused his resignation offer.

9329f8e154dd.headline: Big Bao Swallows Little Bao in a Cosmic Pac-Man Merger Near Andromeda
body: Astronomers have caught a giant star eating its smaller companion on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, according to a new paper in the journal Nature. The merged star has been nicknamed Bao, and it may have been effectively rejuvenated by the meal.

The victim, dubbed Little Bao, had about 0.7 times the mass of the Sun. Its host, Big Bao, was a supergiant roughly seven times the Sun's mass, with a radius 350 times larger and a brightness about 18,000 times greater. Lead author Viraj Karambelkar's team says the pair had orbited each other for thousands of years before the collision.

What makes this special is the timing. Stellar mergers are hard to predict, so they are rarely seen live. The team flagged something odd in February 2023, using data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. Later telescopes tracked the star brightening and shedding dust, and the Zwicky Transient Facility recorded the eruption on 17 October 2025.

The James Webb Space Telescope then observed Bao on 24 December 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. The researchers say that is the earliest follow-up of an event like this. Webb's mid-infrared data revealed the dust the larger star had released over hundreds of years.

The merger also moved fast. Once Little Bao touched the giant's surface, it took only seven orbits, about seven years, to finish the job. Other known mergers involving smaller stars have taken thousands of orbits. Co-author Kishalay De described it as almost like a bomb going off inside a living star.

The process is called common envelope evolution. Sometimes both stars survive and later become neutron stars, black holes, supernovae, gravitational-wave sources or millisecond pulsars. Here, simulations showed Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao's core. Scientists say more observations are needed to pin down Bao's final properties.
9329f8e154dd.summary: Astronomers watched a supergiant star swallow a smaller companion near Andromeda, with the James Webb Space Telescope capturing the aftermath just 47 days after the eruption peaked, according to a new Nature paper.
9329f8e154dd.pixel_take: Little Bao went from binary partner to main course in seven years. Somewhere, a very patient supergiant is still chewing, and astronomers are taking notes.
9329f8e154dd.why_it_matters: Rapid-response space observation is a growing field, and this event shows how coordinated telescope networks and fast data pipelines can catch fleeting events. Better models of stellar mergers also feed into understanding black holes and gravitational waves, which drive long-term science and tech investment.
key_points: A supergiant about 7 times the Sun's mass swallowed a 0.7-solar-mass companion near Andromeda.
Webb observed the merged star, Bao, just 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest such follow-up.
The merger took about seven years, far faster than other known mergers involving smaller stars.

The reference to government consultations is also notable. Nvidia sits at the center of the AI hardware boom, and its chips matter to both commercial customers and national policy. When a company in that position changes leadership, Washington's views can carry real weight.
