87dc9545fdb3.headline: Netflix's FTX drama draws fire as critics note Obama's producer credit and a scene the creator admits he invented
body: Netflix's upcoming drama about the collapse of FTX is facing criticism, with detractors pointing to a producer credit for Barack Obama, according to Cointelegraph. The controversy also centers on a scene the show's creator says he made up.

Series creator Graham Moore said he invented a scene in which Changpeng Zhao, the Binance founder, urges Alameda Research to trade ahead of FTX customers' orders. In other words, the moment was dramatized rather than drawn from a documented event, based on Moore's own account as relayed by Cointelegraph.

The material available to us is brief, so details on the wider criticism, the show's release plans and any response from the people portrayed are not confirmed here. What is clear is the two lightning rods: a famous name in the credits and a fictional scene involving a real, named person.

The dispute is a familiar one for dramas based on real events. Streaming studios compress timelines, merge characters and write dialogue nobody can verify, then tell audiences the result is inspired by the truth. When the subject is a real crypto figure and a scandal involving customer funds, viewers tend to scrutinize those liberties more closely.

Front-running, the practice described in the invented scene, means trading ahead of clients' orders to profit from the price move. Placing such an act in the mouth of a real person, even in fiction, is likely to keep the debate going as the series approaches its audience.
87dc9545fdb3.summary: Critics of Netflix's FTX drama are highlighting Obama's producer credit, while creator Graham Moore admits he invented a scene showing Changpeng Zhao urging Alameda to trade ahead of FTX customers' orders.
87dc9545fdb3.pixel_take: Fiction based on a true story: where the facts take a coffee break and the screenwriter picks up the tab.
87dc9545fdb3.why_it_matters: Popular dramas shape how the public remembers crypto's biggest collapses, and blurred lines between fact and fiction can affect reputations and trust in the industry. For investors, it's a reminder that screen versions of financial scandals are entertainment, not evidence.
key_points: Critics are pointing to Obama's producer credit on Netflix's FTX drama.
Creator Graham Moore said he invented a scene involving Changpeng Zhao and Alameda Research.
The scene depicts urging Alameda to trade ahead of FTX customers' orders.

429094fc08f2.headline: CVS Plans a Breakup, but Antitrust Critics Aren't Letting Go
body: Lawmakers are warning that a planned breakup of CVS Health will not end scrutiny over the company's market power, according to The New York Times. The report, published in late November 2026, describes a spinoff of the health care conglomerate's drugstores that critics say does not resolve their concerns.

The material available is limited: the headline and teaser describe the plan and the pushback, but not the structure, timing or terms of the separation. Those details are not confirmed here, so it is best to treat this as a story about political pressure rather than a finalized deal.

The argument from critics, as the teaser frames it, is that splitting off the drugstores does not by itself shrink the company's influence. In other words, a corporate reorganization is not the same as a cure for the competition worries that lawmakers have raised.

That tension is common in antitrust fights. Companies often argue that separating business units addresses concerns about size and integration. Critics tend to respond that what matters is the power that remains, and whether the pieces still hold sway over prices, patients and rivals.

For CVS, the practical takeaway is that a breakup may not buy it peace with Washington. Lawmakers are signaling that they intend to keep watching, whatever the corporate org chart looks like after the split.
429094fc08f2.summary: Lawmakers say CVS Health's planned spinoff of its drugstores won't end scrutiny of its power, according to The New York Times. Critics see the breakup as not settling their antitrust concerns.
429094fc08f2.pixel_take: CVS is trying to split up to get the regulators off its back. Lawmakers seem to be saying a breakup doesn't count as a clean getaway.
429094fc08f2.why_it_matters: Antitrust pressure on a major health care company can affect its strategy, valuation and how it structures deals. For consumers, scrutiny of such firms bears on competition in health care, which can influence prices and choices.
key_points: Lawmakers say CVS Health's planned drugstore spinoff won't end antitrust scrutiny.
The report comes from The New York Times, published November 2026.
Details of the breakup's structure and timing were not available in the source material.

7238e2f81f4c.headline: Owl Gets Stuck in a Car Grille in North Carolina, Firefighters Pull Off the Rescue
body: Firefighters in North Carolina rescued an owl that became lodged in the front grille of a vehicle, according to UPI. The bird is expected to make a full recovery.

The material available gives few details beyond that. It does not say where exactly the incident happened, what kind of owl it was, or how the bird ended up wedged in the car. Video of the rescue was shared with the report.

Still, the outcome is the part that counts: a trapped wild animal, a team with the right tools and training, and a bird that is expected to be fine. Firefighters are often called for jobs well beyond fires, and freeing an animal from a tight spot is a familiar one.

Wildlife collisions with vehicles are a well-known hazard for birds, especially those that hunt near roads. This one ended better than many, with the owl getting a second chance rather than a trip to the repair shop.
7238e2f81f4c.summary: Firefighters in North Carolina freed an owl stuck in a vehicle's front grille, UPI reported. The bird is expected to fully recover.
7238e2f81f4c.pixel_take: The owl didn't give a hoot about the car's warranty, but it was very glad the firefighters showed up. Tight squeeze, happy ending.

91e0a7d973c2.headline: Arrowmax's AI screwdriver can see your screw, which is more than most of us can say about the instructions
body: Arrowmax is pitching the Arrowspace S1 as the world's first AI screwdriver "with eyes and a brain," according to Digital Trends. A camera in the tip photographs the screw head, software works out the drive type and size, and an optional Smart Case lights up the matching bit. The Kickstarter campaign starts around $79, with shipping promised for April 2027 at the earliest.

The pitch is aimed at anyone who has mangled a laptop screw or forced one into a PC case. Beyond identifying the screw, the S1 offers assisted torque guidance that sets a safer torque, so you are less likely to strip the head.

On the hardware side, a small camera and LED sit at the bottom of the driver next to a precision contact probe that rests on the screw, keeping the lens at a useful focus distance. The detected type and size show up in a companion app, while LEDs in the Smart Case point to the right one of 52 steel bits.

Arrowmax claims a 600mAh battery that lasts up to 90 minutes, or more than 900 screws, plus an OLED screen showing charge level, torque and direction. For context, a basic electric screwdriver kit already costs well under $50.

Pricing is $79 for the driver alone and $129 with the Smart Case on Kickstarter, and retail will be higher. Arrowmax's own shop lists the S1 at HK$1,299 (roughly $166), currently sold out. Arrowmax has run crowdfunding campaigns before, but a pledge is not a store purchase: if the April date slips, backers wait, or may never get a screwdriver.
Then there is the obvious question: do you need AI in a tool that worked fine for decades without it? If yes, you know where your money goes.
91e0a7d973c2.summary: Arrowmax's Arrowspace S1 uses a tip camera and AI to identify screws, light up the right bit and suggest a safe torque. Kickstarter pricing starts near $79, with shipping slated for April 2027.
91e0a7d973c2.pixel_take: A screwdriver that can see the screw, pick the bit and limit the torque. Finally, a tool that reads the manual so you can keep ignoring it.
91e0a7d973c2.why_it_matters: AI is creeping into even the humblest tools, testing whether shoppers will pay a premium for convenience when cheap kits exist. Crowdfunding adds risk: backers fund a promise, not a finished product, and delays or failure are possible.
key_points: The S1 uses a tip camera and AI to identify screw type and size, then lights the matching bit in the optional Smart Case.
Kickstarter pricing is $79 for the driver and $129 with the case, with shipping in April 2027 at the earliest.
A pledge is not a purchase, so backers bear the risk of delays or non-delivery.

4fc9328efd4a.headline: Vegas Grand Prix Turns Into F1's Version of an Oval Race, With 35 Lead Changes and a Ferrari Meltdown
body: Formula 1's Las Vegas Grand Prix, run on the city's streets this past weekend, finally delivered the spectacle it had promised since 2023. According to Ars Technica, the race featured 352 position changes, including 35 for the lead, and looked more like an IndyCar oval event than a typical modern F1 race.

Max Verstappen took his 75th career win for Red Bull. Lando Norris finished just 0.64 seconds behind in his McLaren, with teammate Oscar Piastri a similar gap further back. The two McLarens worked well together and collected a big haul of points in their fight with Ferrari for second in the constructors' standings.

The ingredients were unusual. Las Vegas has long straights but mostly slow corners, and a cold night with a track temperature of about 59°F (15°C) meant low grip but almost no tire wear or overheating. The new aerodynamic rules also made the slipstream far stronger, so five or six cars were often covered by about 2.5 seconds. Picking the right moment to attack mattered a lot, because a bad call could cost several places at once.

Verstappen and George Russell of Mercedes swapped the lead repeatedly after a clean start, with Russell passing on the straights and Verstappen retaking the position in the corners. Mercedes then fumbled. Russell hit a barrier on lap 47, probably after running over debris from Isack Hadjar's broken front wing, and Kimi Antonelli drained his battery instead of saving energy for a last-lap pass. Hadjar, running third, had dropped to last when his wing failed on lap 25.

Ferrari had the worst of it. Neither car made the final qualifying session, and in the race Charles Leclerc tried to pass teammate Lewis Hamilton despite being told to hold position, causing contact. Stewards blamed Leclerc and gave him a 10-second penalty. Hamilton finished seventh and Leclerc tenth.

Verstappen was also in a spiky mood afterward, saying Russell was far below his level. Ars Technica notes that conditions in Vegas were unique, so the next two Middle East rounds are unlikely to look similar.
4fc9328efd4a.summary: Las Vegas delivered a wild F1 race with 352 position changes and 35 lead changes. Verstappen won, Mercedes fumbled, and Ferrari's Leclerc cost teammate Hamilton points with a failed pass.
4fc9328efd4a.pixel_take: Thirty-five lead changes and Ferrari still found a way to lose to itself. Even in a race where everyone was drafting, only Leclerc and Hamilton managed to crash into teamwork.
4fc9328efd4a.why_it_matters: F1 is a huge global entertainment business, and exciting races like this help sell the Las Vegas event, broadcast rights and sponsorship deals. Points lost to team errors also matter in the constructors' standings, where prize money is tied to final position.
key_points: The race had 352 position changes, including 35 for the lead.
Verstappen won ahead of Norris and Piastri after Mercedes errors.
Leclerc's penalized pass on Hamilton cost Ferrari points.

a19c022caec4.headline: Tajikistan Heads for the ICC Exit as Fourth Country to Quit Since US Urged Departures
body: Tajikistan has formally told the United Nations it is withdrawing from the International Criminal Court, according to Al Jazeera. The ICC's governing body has expressed concern. The exit from the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the court, is due to take effect on November 20, 2027.

Tajikistan is the fourth country to start the withdrawal process since the United States urged nations in July to leave the tribunal. Venezuela, Chad and Naoero, the Pacific nation formerly known as Nauru, have already begun the same process.

The timing is awkward for the court. In March, the ICC found that Tajikistan had failed to comply with its request to arrest Russian President Vladimir Putin when he visited in 2025. Putin is wanted over alleged war crimes in Ukraine.

Washington's pushback is also a major backdrop. The Trump administration has sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors over the court's 2024 arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant, which relate to alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and over an earlier probe into US forces in Afghanistan. In July, the State Department said it would seek to disable the court's operations, calling it an enforcement arm of a "globalist bureaucracy".

Tajikistan is not the only exit in the pipeline. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger announced plans to leave in 2025, calling the court an instrument of "neocolonial repression", and notified the UN in June, before the US campaign began. All seven countries with pending withdrawals remain among the ICC's 125 member states. The US, Russia, China, Israel and India are not members.
a19c022caec4.summary: Tajikistan has notified the UN it is leaving the ICC, effective November 2027, becoming the fourth country to start withdrawing since the US urged exits in July. The ICC has voiced concern.
a19c022caec4.why_it_matters: A shrinking membership could weaken the court's reach and the global rules-based approach to prosecuting war crimes. For markets and businesses, it signals growing geopolitical fragmentation, with sanctions and legal pressure becoming tools of foreign policy.
key_points: Tajikistan's ICC withdrawal takes effect on November 20, 2027.
It is the fourth country to begin leaving since the US urged exits in July, after Venezuela, Chad and Naoero.
The ICC found in March that Tajikistan failed to arrest Putin during his 2025 visit.

2051fbe57206.headline: ACEMAGIC's 1985-Looking Retro X5 Mini PC Drops $300 for Black Friday
body: ACEMAGIC's Retro X5 gaming mini PC is on sale for Black Friday at $899.99, down $300 (25%) from its $1,199.99 list price, according to Digital Trends. The deal is listed on Amazon and on ACEMAGIC's official store at the same price.

The pitch is a machine that looks like it escaped from 1985, with a vintage gray shell and mechanical grille vents, but runs modern hardware. Inside is an AMD Ryzen AI 9 365 processor with 10 cores and 20 threads, boosting up to 5.0GHz, plus 32GB of LPDDR5X memory and a 1TB NVMe SSD. A tool-free top cover lets owners expand storage to 8TB without a screwdriver.

Graphics come from the integrated Radeon 880M, which Digital Trends says handles modern AAA games at 1080p with FSR. It is also pitched as an emulation station for retro libraries through Batocera or RetroArch. So the beige-box nostalgia is not just for show.

The other selling point is AI. With a dedicated NPU and 73 total TOPS, the system can reportedly run 7B to 14B large language models offline, with no subscription. Connectivity includes quad 8K/4K display outputs, front USB4, dual 2.5GbE LAN ports and Wi-Fi 6E.

The system ships with Windows 11 Pro pre-installed and a two-year warranty. Digital Trends argues that building a comparable custom Mini-ITX PC gets expensive quickly, which makes the turnkey price attractive. As usual with Black Friday, the discount may not last long.
2051fbe57206.summary: ACEMAGIC's retro-styled Retro X5 mini PC, with a Ryzen AI 9 365 and 32GB of RAM, is $899.99 for Black Friday, $300 off its list price, per Digital Trends.
2051fbe57206.pixel_take: It looks like it should run a floppy disk and a screensaver of flying toasters, yet it hosts offline AI models. Your desk gets a time machine, and your wallet gets a $300 head start.
2051fbe57206.why_it_matters: Small form factor PCs with built-in AI hardware are becoming a real alternative to bulky desktops and cloud subscriptions. Running language models locally can save recurring fees, and Black Friday pricing shows how competitive the mini PC market has become.
key_points: The Retro X5 is $899.99, $300 (25%) off its $1,199.99 list price, on Amazon and ACEMAGIC's store.
It packs a Ryzen AI 9 365, 32GB LPDDR5X, a 1TB SSD and 73 total TOPS of AI performance.
It ships with Windows 11 Pro and a two-year warranty, and storage expands to 8TB.

6846508d0d79.headline: Cuomo says rivals nudged companies to skip OKXICE's tokenized stocks rollout
body: Former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo says competitors encouraged companies to opt out of the rollout of OKXICE's tokenized stocks, according to Cointelegraph. The claim surfaced on November 23, 2026.
Per the same report, Cuomo added that not every issuer who stepped back was swayed by rivals. Some simply wanted more time before having their shares appear in tokenized form.

The material available is thin. It does not say which competitors Cuomo means, which companies opted out, or what form the alleged encouragement took. Those claims remain unverified and should be read as Cuomo's account, not established fact.

Some context helps. Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based tokens designed to track the price of traditional shares, and they are a hot battleground in crypto because they promise round-the-clock trading and wider access. Whether a listed company is comfortable seeing its shares tokenized by a third party is a delicate question, so opt-out options matter.

If competitors really are lobbying issuers to step aside, it would show how fiercely platforms are fighting for early position in this young market. If the hesitation is mostly about timing, as Cuomo also suggests, it points to the slower, more cautious pace that established companies often take with new financial plumbing.
6846508d0d79.summary: Andrew Cuomo says competitors urged companies to opt out of OKXICE's tokenized stocks rollout, while some issuers just wanted more time, according to Cointelegraph.
6846508d0d79.pixel_take: Nothing says a market is worth winning like rivals politely suggesting everyone sit this one out. Meanwhile, some companies just want a few more minutes in the changing room.
6846508d0d79.why_it_matters: Tokenized stocks could change how people trade shares, so a fight over who gets listed shapes which products reach investors. Issuer hesitation also signals how far traditional companies are willing to go onchain.
key_points: Cuomo says rivals encouraged companies to opt out of OKXICE's tokenized stocks.
Some issuers reportedly just wanted more time.
Details on companies and competitors were not provided.

fdf18ad95019.headline: Jeffries Vows to Bench Congress's Stock Portfolios 'Very Early' in the Next Congress
body: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), widely seen as the next House Speaker, said Sunday on CBS's Face the Nation that House Democrats will move to ban members of Congress from trading stocks "very early" in the new Congress.

Asked by host Margaret Brennan about his agenda, Jeffries said Washington needs a cleanup that covers Congress, the Supreme Court and the administration. He said the effort should start with Congress itself, according to The Hill.

The pledge follows Democratic wins in the House and Senate in the midterm elections earlier this month, including victories in places like Texas and Kansas where the party has historically struggled. Last Wednesday, House Democrats nominated Jeffries for Speaker, with 251 votes from his caucus and 11 against. He would be the chamber's first Black Speaker.

The idea has a tangled recent history. In late September, Senate Democrats blocked the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would have stopped members from buying new stocks of publicly traded companies. The vote was 53-47, short of the 60 needed, with no Democrats in favor. They argued the bill did not do enough to guard against possible corruption.

Stock trading is not the only item on Jeffries's list. He also wants to reverse Medicaid cuts adopted by Republicans last year and to expand ObamaCare tax credits, which Republicans let expire at the start of 2026, according to the report.
fdf18ad95019.summary: Hakeem Jeffries, likely the next House Speaker, says House Democrats will move to ban lawmakers from trading stocks very early in the next Congress, after Democrats' midterm wins and a failed Senate bill in September.
fdf18ad95019.pixel_take: Congress may soon have to pick between passing laws and picking stocks. Voters will be watching which one they were actually hired to do.
fdf18ad95019.why_it_matters: Lawmakers vote on rules that can move whole industries, so their personal trades have long fueled suspicion of conflicts of interest. A real ban could reshape how politicians handle their money and affect trust in markets and government. Details, such as whether it covers new purchases only, will matter.
key_points: Jeffries says House Democrats will move to ban member stock trading early in the new Congress.
A Senate bill on the topic failed 53-47 in September, short of the 60 votes needed.
Medicaid cuts and ObamaCare tax credits are also on his agenda.

39e3d33fb9cf.headline: Voyager 1 hits one light-day from Earth, the farthest any human-made object has ever strayed
body: NASA's Voyager 1 probe has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth, according to UPI. That makes it the first human-made object in space to get that far from home.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, so a signal from Voyager 1 now needs a full day to cross the gap. Send it a message and you will wait roughly a day for it to arrive, then another day for the reply.

The milestone caps a decades-long journey. UPI reports that the probe has explored both the solar system and the interstellar medium beyond it, the thin space between stars that lies outside the Sun's immediate influence.

The material available for this story is brief, so details on the exact date of the crossing and the probe's current condition are not covered here. The headline fact is simple: nothing built by humans has ever been this far away.

For context, Voyager 1 is a veteran of an era when spacecraft were built to last on very modest computing power. It is a reminder that long-term engineering, patience and a good dose of luck can outlast several generations of gadgets, most of which struggle to survive a phone upgrade cycle.
39e3d33fb9cf.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth, a distance light needs 24 hours to cross, according to UPI.
39e3d33fb9cf.pixel_take: Voyager 1 is so far away that even its replies to 'u up?' arrive a day late. Still more reliable than most of our gadgets after two years.
39e3d33fb9cf.why_it_matters: Voyager 1 shows the payoff of long-horizon investment in space science and engineering durability. Data from interstellar space can't be gathered any other way, and it informs future deep-space mission design, a field with growing commercial and government interest.
key_points: Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth, a first for any human-made object.
Signals take about 24 hours to travel one way at that distance.
The probe has explored both the solar system and interstellar space, per UPI.

9047326037c9.headline: Three extra screens, zero chill: tri-screen portable monitor tested
body: Ars Technica has tested KYY's X90G, a portable monitor with three 15.6-inch IPS screens that clamp around a laptop, and the verdict is mixed. It can turn a small desk into a four-screen command center, but the reviewer found it distracting and bulky. It costs $360 as of the review.

Each panel runs at 1920x1080 and is rated for up to 400 nits of brightness. One screen sits on each side of the laptop and one above it, which Ars says makes for a more cohesive layout than rivals that stack all three above the laptop. It works with Windows, macOS (on M1 chips or better), Linux and Android. Laptops larger than 17.3 inches won't fit.

The tester says the setup never felt like one big display. The screens don't line up in a row, so moving the mouse between them can be awkward. Bezels and parts of the back panel also stayed visible, and the lit screen above the laptop kept pulling the reviewer's eyes away. With a 13-inch laptop, a gap and handle opening sat between the laptop screen and the top monitor.

There are upsides. Each screen tilts independently and has its own menu, controls and power button, so one can be dimmed for writing while another is brightened for photo editing. The side panels made it easy to keep reports, spreadsheets and photos in view during research, and the top screen worked for email, chat or a Finnish puppy cam.

Space and portability are the catch. Fully extended, the X90G is about 46 inches wide, wider than the reviewer's desk, and it weighs 6.4 pounds, more than twice the weight of the ultralight Dell XPS laptop used in testing. On days when it stayed set up, plugging in one USB-C cable to light up three extra screens felt pretty magical.
The conclusion: it suits people who want to share information or juggle many tasks, but for those who just want more transportable screen space or a tidy workspace, three screens may be overkill.
9047326037c9.summary: Ars Technica tested KYY's $360 X90G, a three-screen portable monitor. It offers lots of multitasking room, but separate-feeling displays, distraction, 46-inch width and 6.4-pound weight make it overkill for many users.
9047326037c9.pixel_take: Four screens and still no way to stop staring at the puppy cam. The pixels multiplied; the attention span stayed exactly where it was.
9047326037c9.why_it_matters: Remote and hybrid work keeps pushing people to spend on gear that squeezes more productivity from small spaces. This review is a reminder that more pixels don't automatically mean more output, so check your actual workflow before spending $360.
key_points: KYY's X90G adds three 15.6-inch 1080p screens around a laptop for $360.
Screens feel like separate displays, and the top one can distract.
It's about 46 inches wide and 6.4 pounds, limiting true portability.

abb5957252d7.headline: Bitcoin ETFs Bleed $1.8B in Third-Largest Weekly Outflow Ever
body: Investors pulled about $1.8 billion out of Bitcoin exchange-traded funds in the latest week, marking the third-largest weekly outflow on record, according to Cointelegraph. The report covers flows through Friday and was published on November 23, 2026.

The weekly exodus pushed November's total outflows to $4.14 billion, with the month not yet finished. That figure is closing in on June's $4.51 billion, per the same report, which suggests November could soon claim a spot among the heavier months for withdrawals.

The material available does not spell out why money is leaving, so it would be unwise to pin the blame on any single cause. What the numbers do show is a clear shift in sentiment among the investors who use these funds, which let people gain Bitcoin exposure through ordinary brokerage accounts without holding the coins themselves.

Context matters here. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have become a key channel for institutional and retail demand, so their flows are closely watched as a mood ring for the market. Sustained outflows can mean funds are selling underlying Bitcoin to meet redemptions, which can add pressure to prices, though the link is not always one for one.

For now, the story is one of momentum running in reverse. If November's outflows pass June's $4.51 billion, the month would rank as an even sharper retreat. Whether this proves a short wobble or a longer cooling-off will depend on whether the withdrawals continue in the coming weeks.
abb5957252d7.summary: Bitcoin ETFs lost $1.8 billion in their third-largest weekly outflow, per Cointelegraph. November's outflows hit $4.14 billion through Friday, close to June's $4.51 billion total.
abb5957252d7.pixel_take: Bitcoin ETF investors are heading for the exits so fast you'd think someone yelled 'free pizza' in the parking lot. November is eyeing June's record like a runner spotting the finish line.
abb5957252d7.why_it_matters: ETF flows are a key gauge of institutional appetite for Bitcoin, and heavy outflows can add selling pressure to the market. Anyone holding crypto or crypto-linked funds should watch whether the trend persists or fades.
key_points: Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.8B in weekly outflows, the third-largest ever.
November outflows total $4.14B through Friday.
June's $4.51B total is the mark November is approaching.

aa60aee61556.headline: California AG Says Huang Reinstatement Changes Nothing, According to Investing.com
body: California's attorney general has said that the reinstatement of someone named Huang does not change the state's position, according to a headline from Investing.com published on November 23, 2026.

That is essentially all the material available. The original article text and teaser were not provided, so key details remain unclear: who Huang is, what he or she was reinstated to, and which matter the attorney general's office is addressing.

What the headline does tell us is the tone of the response. In legal and regulatory disputes, a statement that a development 'changes nothing' usually signals that an office intends to keep pursuing its existing course, whether that is an investigation, a lawsuit or a policy stance.

Because the story was filed under markets, it may carry implications for a company or its investors. Without more reporting, though, any specific market impact would be speculation, and PixelContent will update if fuller details become available.
aa60aee61556.summary: California's attorney general says the reinstatement of Huang changes nothing, per an Investing.com headline. Further details were not available in the material provided.
aa60aee61556.pixel_take: When an attorney general says a big comeback 'changes nothing,' that's the legal equivalent of a raised eyebrow with a badge attached.
aa60aee61556.why_it_matters: Regulatory stances from a state attorney general can shape risk for companies and investors, even when the headlines are brief. Until fuller details emerge, readers should treat the market impact as unclear rather than assume either direction.

The report comes from an Investing.com headline dated November 23, 2026.
Details on who Huang is and the underlying matter were not provided.

df6ffd1d4725.headline: Iran Vows 'All Available Means' Against US Naval Blockade as Hormuz Standoff Drags On
body: Iran said on Monday it will use "all available means" to counter a US naval blockade, according to Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, who spoke at a news briefing. The blockade is part of a nine-month war involving the United States, Israel and Iran.

Baghaei argued that what Washington calls economic sanctions and a naval blockade amount to military aggression. He said Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers self-defense, entitles Iran to respond with any means available.

The blockade began on April 13, was lifted in June after the US and Iran reached a draft understanding, and was reimposed on July 14 when that agreement collapsed, Al Jazeera reported. The war itself began on February 28 with US-Israeli air strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials. It has since widened, with Iranian missile and drone attacks across the region and involvement from armed groups in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq.

The Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil and natural gas shipments, is at the center of the dispute. Iran has kept trying to block the waterway, and the US responded with the port blockade, further sanctions and a task force aimed at disrupting land routes into Iran. Iranian forces have also announced that ships caught fire in recent weeks while using routes Tehran considers off-limits.

The economic squeeze appears real. Visible Iranian crude exports have fallen to near zero in recent months. TankerTrackers.com said last week that a tanker loading Iranian crude via ship-to-ship transfer might be the first to export successfully since July, but Baghaei called such reports speculation. Al Jazeera's correspondent in Tehran noted that more than 80 percent of Iran's imports and exports move through Hormuz or southern ports, and that military action against US assets is being discussed.
Diplomacy remains stalled. Iran says Hormuz could reopen within two days if Washington halts hostilities, lifts the blockade and waives sanctions.
df6ffd1d4725.summary: Iran says it will use all available means against the US naval blockade, calling it military aggression. Hormuz remains contested, Iranian oil exports are near zero and talks are stalled.
df6ffd1d4725.why_it_matters: Hormuz carries a large share of the world's oil and gas, so any prolonged disruption can push up energy prices and shake markets. Near-zero Iranian exports and the threat of military escalation add risk for shipping, insurance and inflation worldwide.
key_points: Iran says the US blockade is military aggression and cites Article 51 of the UN Charter.
The blockade was imposed April 13, lifted in June, and reimposed July 14 after a deal collapsed.
Visible Iranian crude exports are near zero, and Iran says Hormuz could reopen in two days if its conditions are met.

89e5b94b9291.headline: Merach RS3 Dual-Oar Rower Drops to $305.99, Doubling as a Cable Station
body: The Merach RS3 Scull Rowing Machine is currently $305.99 on Amazon, a 15% cut from its $359.99 list price, according to Digital Trends. It is a home-gym rower with a twist: two separate oars instead of one straight bar.

That design is the selling point. The RS3 uses independent dual oars on a 120-degree stroke arc, which Digital Trends says makes your core and stabilizer muscles work differently to keep rhythm, and more closely mimics sculling on water than a standard bar-pull rower does.

Resistance comes from a magnetic system with 16 selectable levels. It is described as silent, which matters if you live in an apartment or share space and a loud air rower would turn every workout into a neighborhood announcement. The machine also pairs with the Merach App, which logs metrics, tracks personal records and offers structured training classes.

The second trick is versatility. Because the machine works with standard gym handles, you can swap attachments and perform more than 26 resistance movements, effectively turning it into a compact cable station. Digital Trends says that lets you target nearly 90% of your muscle groups without buying a separate functional trainer.
As always with discounts on fitness gear, the deal may not last, so check the current price before buying. The figures above come from the Digital Trends report, not from independent testing.
89e5b94b9291.summary: The Merach RS3 Scull Rowing Machine is $305.99 on Amazon, 15% off its $359.99 list price. It pairs dual-oar rowing with cable-style workouts and quiet magnetic resistance, according to Digital Trends.
89e5b94b9291.pixel_take: Two oars, 26-plus exercises, and no air-rower roar. Your downstairs neighbors get a quiet workout too, and your wallet gets a modest rowing-sized break.
89e5b94b9291.why_it_matters: Home fitness gear is a big budget item, and a machine that replaces two devices can save both money and floor space. Discounts like this show how retailers compete for gadget shoppers heading into the holiday season.
key_points: The Merach RS3 is $305.99 on Amazon, 15% off the $359.99 list price.
It uses dual oars on a 120-degree arc and quiet magnetic resistance with 16 levels.
It doubles as a cable station for more than 26 exercises and pairs with the Merach App.

92effb5a3302.headline: Wired Wants Your Toughest Questions on AI Safety, and Who Is Actually Minding the Store
body: Wired is inviting readers to submit questions for a livestream on December 2 about a simple but unsettling topic: will anyone keep people safe from artificial intelligence? The magazine's Backchannel team will answer questions about Big Tech and AI safety, according to a post published November 23.

The framing is blunt. Wired says experts broadly agree that AI poses real danger, even if they disagree on which catastrophe deserves the most worry. The list it offers runs from the dramatic, such as the technology killing everyone, to the practical, such as cyberattacks by rogue agents and a wider societal collapse.

The central question is what industry leaders are doing about risks they helped unleash. Wired notes that several ideas have been floated, including a pause in training models, a moratorium on data centers and other forms of regulation. But the magazine argues that the industry has not made changes that put people at ease.

Meanwhile, Wired says critical infrastructure looks more vulnerable by the day. That is the part worth watching for anyone who doesn't care about sci-fi doom scenarios: power grids, hospitals and financial systems are the places where an AI-assisted attack would hurt in everyday ways.

The livestream is part of Wired's ongoing series assessing the real threats of AI, and it follows earlier sessions on women in tech, the defense tech industry and the future of electric vehicles. The post doesn't name guests or announce any new findings, so this is an invitation to a conversation rather than a news event in itself.

Still, the premise reflects a growing tension. Companies race to ship ever more capable systems while governments debate rules, and the public is left wondering who holds the brakes. Wired is betting that readers have questions, and it is offering a stage for them.
92effb5a3302.summary: Wired is collecting reader questions for a December 2 livestream on AI safety, asking what industry leaders are doing about the risks and whether regulation or pauses will materialize.
92effb5a3302.pixel_take: Asking whether anyone will keep you safe from AI is a bit like asking who is driving the bus. Wired suspects the answer is a shrug, and it's taking questions.
92effb5a3302.why_it_matters: AI safety debates shape regulation, data center buildout and corporate spending, all of which affect tech valuations and energy costs. Vulnerable infrastructure is also a direct risk to businesses and household finances if attacks succeed.
key_points: Wired hosts an AI safety livestream on December 2 and is taking reader questions.
Proposals like a training pause and a data center moratorium have surfaced, but Wired says industry changes haven't reassured people.
Wired flags critical infrastructure as increasingly vulnerable.

d5056aa77c07.headline: London's Newest Estate Agent Sells Gingerbread Homes, and the Only Mortgage Is Your Sweet Tooth
body: A gingerbread 'estate agent' has opened in Bloomsbury, central London, offering visitors a look at miniature edible houses. According to Metro, the pop-up, called Crumbs, Coffee & Co, opens on November 18 at 43 Store Street.

The tiny properties were made by baker Jenny Pasha, who spent 150 hours crafting houses that reflect popular architectural styles found across London. The star attraction is a model of the Shard, which on its own took 60 hours of baking and building.

The project is a promotional stunt from Nescafé. The brand says a survey found Brits name gingerbread as their favourite winter flavour, ahead of cinnamon, salted caramel, pumpkin spice and spiced apple.

The timing is deliberate: Nescafé is bringing back its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after a ten-year break, which it says followed fan petitions and social media requests. Visitors can collect a freshly brewed one for free, and entry to the pop-up costs nothing.

Ingrid Hayes, marketing director for Nescafé UK and Ireland, said research shows people want simple, affordable ways to bring joy to their winter routine. She said the pop-up gives fans an immersive way to celebrate the flavour while bringing café-style warmth into their own kitchens.
d5056aa77c07.summary: Nescafé has opened a free gingerbread 'estate agent' pop-up in Bloomsbury, London, showing handmade edible houses and a Shard model, to launch the return of its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after ten years.
d5056aa77c07.pixel_take: Finally, a London property with no bidding wars, no chain collapses and no survey needed. The only damp is the icing, and the only deposit is a latte you get free.
d5056aa77c07.why_it_matters: Brands are leaning on immersive pop-ups and nostalgia to make seasonal products feel like events, often cheaper than traditional advertising and perfect for social sharing. For shoppers, it shows how consumer sentiment about 'affordable joy' is shaping marketing in the coffee aisle.
key_points: Crumbs, Coffee & Co opens November 18 at 43 Store Street, Bloomsbury, with free entry.
Baker Jenny Pasha spent 150 hours on the houses, including 60 hours on a Shard replica.
Nescafé is reviving its Gingerbread Flavour Latte after ten years and giving away free cups.

c5c49f64212c.headline: Trump Renews Call for Nvidia to 'Rehire' Jensen Huang as CEO
body: President Donald Trump has renewed his call for Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as chief executive, according to a report from Cointelegraph. The message came in a Truth Social post on Monday, in which Trump said bringing Huang back would be good for both the chipmaker and the United States.

The material available gives only that bare outline. The headline and teaser do not explain the circumstances behind the call, and they do not say whether Huang has left the role, been replaced, or whether the post refers to something else. We also don't have the wording of the post beyond the teaser's summary, and no response from Nvidia or Huang was included.

The word "renews" signals that this is not the first time Trump has raised the idea, but details of any earlier comments were not provided. Readers should treat the story as a developing item until more context emerges from Nvidia, Huang or the White House.

Even so, the post shows how closely political leaders now watch the biggest names in tech. Nvidia sits at the center of the AI hardware boom, and its leadership is a matter of interest well beyond Silicon Valley, from investors to policymakers. When a president comments publicly on who should run a company of that profile, markets and executives tend to pay attention.
For now, the confirmed facts are limited: a Truth Social post, a Monday timing, a call for Huang to be rehired as CEO, and Trump's claim that it would benefit Nvidia and the country.
c5c49f64212c.summary: Trump used a Truth Social post on Monday to again urge Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO, saying it would help both the company and the US, per Cointelegraph. Context remains unclear.
c5c49f64212c.pixel_take: When a presidential post tells a company to rehire its CEO, the real mystery is the plot. The teaser gives us the cliffhanger and skips the previous episodes.
c5c49f64212c.why_it_matters: Nvidia is a key company in AI and chips, so public comments from a president about its leadership can draw investor attention. The story is thin on details, so it is a reminder to wait for confirmation before reacting with your portfolio.
key_points: Trump posted on Truth Social on Monday urging Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO.
He said the move would benefit both Nvidia and the US.
The source gave no background on the circumstances or any reaction from Nvidia.

ea3dbf01cc50.headline: COP31 Ends in Collapse as Fossil Fuel Wording Sinks the Antalya Pact
body: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended without a deal after delegates failed to agree on a final declaration, the Antalya Pact. According to BBC News, the sticking point was the mention of fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming, though deeper geopolitical and financial rifts lay beneath it.

The draft pact did not mention fossil fuels at all. That stood out because three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to transition away from them. Countries that rejected the text feared it would weaken the Dubai commitment. About 130 governments, roughly two-thirds of those present, backed explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels.

Opposition came openly from oil-producing nations. A Saudi negotiator speaking for the 22 Arab League countries said Arab states had contributed less than 2% of historical emissions and should choose their own path. Russia's delegate warned that cutting supply before demand falls would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty, and said Russia could not accept any fossil fuel formulation.

The US sent no official delegation, as President Donald Trump has rejected the international climate process. Meanwhile, Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. Chris Bowen, who co-led the talks, cited the most fraught geopolitical environment in living memory.

Money was the second fault line. Russia attacked the EU over climate finance, arguing that much of it comes as loans rather than grants. Many developing countries share that complaint. The EU had ruled out significant new funding beforehand, and campaigner Mohamed Adow accused Europe of ignoring its own responsibility for the finance failure.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell has called for the process to be reformed and modernised. Ideas include voting when consensus fails, or letting willing countries move faster outside the formal talks. Critics note that climate cooperation is voluntary and that consensus protects smaller nations. Notably, the draft still voiced deep concern that warming would pass 1.5°C within a few years, and that language apparently drew no objection.
ea3dbf01cc50.summary: The COP31 summit in Antalya ended with no deal after a row over fossil fuel wording, a US boycott and a dispute over climate finance. Most governments wanted stronger language, but consensus rules let a few block it.
ea3dbf01cc50.why_it_matters: Without a global deal, businesses and investors get little policy certainty on fossil fuels or climate finance. The energy transition continues on cost grounds, as solar, batteries and EVs get more competitive, but not at the pace climate goals require.
key_points: COP31 in Antalya ended with no deal after the Antalya Pact omitted fossil fuels and was rejected.
About 130 governments backed explicit fossil fuel language, while oil producers like Saudi Arabia and Russia resisted.
Climate finance disputes and a US boycott deepened the split, prompting calls to reform the consensus-based process.

ee5aa285a746.headline: Tiny Fire Ants Keep Beating a Rival Three Times Their Size, and Strategy Is Why
body: Researchers in China have worked out how fire ants manage to defeat an invasive rival ant that is more than three times their size, according to Gizmodo. The short version: they win by working smarter, not harder.

The details of the fighting method are not available in the material we received, so we will not guess at the tactics. What the report makes clear is that raw size does not decide these battles. The smaller species has a game plan, and it appears to be a good one.

It is a familiar underdog story. In nature, as in business, the bigger player does not always win. A nimble competitor with better coordination or smarter tactics can beat an opponent that simply has more mass.

Invasive species are a real economic concern. Aggressive ants can damage crops, infrastructure and ecosystems, and managing them costs money. Understanding why one species beats another could help scientists predict how invasions play out and which species may hold the others in check.
For now, the takeaway is modest but fun: in the ant world, brains and tactics can beat brawn. Further details of the study would be needed to say exactly how the fire ants pull it off.
ee5aa285a746.summary: Researchers in China have figured out how fire ants beat an invasive ant more than three times their size, according to Gizmodo. Their edge comes from smarter tactics, not brute strength.
ee5aa285a746.pixel_take: Fire ants bring a strategy to a size fight and win. Somewhere, a very large rival ant is rethinking its entire business model.
ee5aa285a746.why_it_matters: Invasive species can harm agriculture, infrastructure and ecosystems, which carries real costs. Knowing how one species outcompetes another could help in forecasting and managing infestations. It is also a reminder that scale is not everything in a contest.
key_points: Researchers in China studied how fire ants beat a larger invasive ant.
The rival ant is more than three times the size of the fire ants.
The winning edge is smarter tactics, not greater strength, per Gizmodo.

efc83263c6cf.headline: Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia, and Wall Street Exhales (For Now)
body: U.S. stocks surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, offering investors a breather after a punishing stretch. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite had all closed Friday in correction territory, according to CNBC.

The S&P 500 alone fell more than 9% between Nov. 12, when Huang's departure was first announced, and Friday's close. Monday's bounce prompted strategists to ask whether the worst is behind the market, at least in the short run.

Mark Gibbens of Gibbens Capital Management said he believes the news sets a bottom and a floor for the AI trade. He pointed to Nvidia's role as a keystone, both in financing the AI build-out and in the technology's supply chain, so a steadier Nvidia means a sunnier market outlook.

Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth Management argued the bottom may have been forming already. Friday's selling hit sectors well beyond AI, a sign of exhaustion, and futures were higher Sunday night before any Huang news. He also noted that tech trades at 16.3 times forward earnings versus 20.5 for consumer staples, per FactSet, a gap he says doesn't match earnings prospects.

Not everyone is popping champagne. Jay Woods of Freedom Capital Markets called it a counter-trend rally in a near-term downtrend, expecting it to fizzle because the old questions remain, though he thinks the year's lows are likely in. Peter Boockvar of One Point BFG Wealth Partners remains wary of the 'picks and shovels' AI names, saying their fate hinges on the pace of capital spending.

The sell-off began before the Huang drama, driven by worries over financing the AI build-out, data center approvals after Democratic midterm wins, and fears that hyperscaler capex has peaked or soon will. Those issues did not disappear with one executive announcement.
efc83263c6cf.summary: Stocks rallied after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as CEO, and some strategists see a market bottom. Others warn that AI spending, financing and data-center worries still threaten the rebound.
efc83263c6cf.pixel_take: One CEO memo and the S&P gets its groove back. Markets say they trade on fundamentals, but sometimes they just want a familiar face and a leather-jacket-shaped security blanket.
efc83263c6cf.why_it_matters: Nvidia sits at the center of the AI trade that has powered this bull market, so its leadership news can swing broad indexes and retirement portfolios. The real test is whether AI capital spending keeps growing, which matters more than any single headline.
key_points: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq rallied Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, following a correction; the S&P fell over 9% from Nov. 12 to Friday.
Some strategists see a bottom, citing oversold conditions and cheaper tech valuations versus consumer staples.
Skeptics warn the rally may fade as capex, financing and data-center approval worries persist.

cd38cf9ef5db.headline: Pentagon Brass Pack the Pews at DC Church Run by Pastor Who Wants Women's Vote Repealed
body: Christ Church DC, a congregation that opened on Capitol Hill about a year ago, has become a regular Sunday stop for senior US government officials, according to a Wired investigation. Wired says it identified around a dozen officials who have attended at least once, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who regularly worships with his family.

The church belongs to the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), a network founded by Idaho pastor Doug Wilson, headquartered in Moscow, Idaho. Wired reports that Wilson wants America to become a theocracy governed by biblical law, with non-Christians barred from office and women submitting to their husbands rather than voting. He advocated repealing the 19th Amendment as recently as 2024, according to the report. Wilson calls Washington "Babylon on the Potomac."

Hegseth is the link. He moved his family to the Nashville area in 2022 to attend a CREC church. After his confirmation, he started a monthly Pentagon prayer service and brought in his Tennessee pastor, Brooks Potteiger, to lead the first one. Potteiger became pastor of Christ Church DC in July. Wired says Hegseth has also invited Wilson to speak at Pentagon prayer sessions twice this year.

Other worshippers named by Wired include Justin Overbaugh, a deputy undersecretary for intelligence and security, and Nate Halverson, a chief of staff in the Navy's manpower office who graduated from a Moscow, Idaho college Wilson cofounded. The list also includes Navy counselor Sonny Duncan, Pentagon adviser Stuart Scheller and Ryan Higgins, a senior adviser on religious issues. Wired also lists a top international health diplomat and a federal immigration judge among attendees.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told Wired that Hegseth is a proud member of a CREC-affiliated church and appreciates many of Wilson's writings. He added that staff are free to attend any church and called the story a smear of personnel exercising religious freedom. Wilson agreed to an interview, then canceled, and the church did not respond to Wired's request for comment.
cd38cf9ef5db.summary: Wired reports that senior Pentagon and government officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, attend Christ Church DC, part of a network led by pastor Doug Wilson, who advocates theocracy. The Pentagon calls the story a smear.
cd38cf9ef5db.why_it_matters: Who sits in the pews alongside who shapes policy conversations in Washington, especially at the Pentagon, which controls a vast budget and personnel decisions. Religion in government is a live political issue that can influence defense policy, hiring and public trust in institutions.
key_points: Wired identified around a dozen officials who have attended Christ Church DC since it opened a year ago.
The church is tied to Doug Wilson's CREC network, and Hegseth brought his pastor into the Pentagon.
The Pentagon says staff may worship freely and accuses Wired of smearing personnel.

d8f91bd27568.headline: Sheep on the Lam: Fugitive Flock-Member Eludes Connecticut Police and Animal Wranglers for Days
body: A sheep that bolted shortly after arriving at its new owner's home in Connecticut remains at large, according to UPI. Police and animal wranglers say the animal has not been seen in days, despite efforts to track it down.

The details are thin: the material available does not say where in Connecticut the escape happened, how the sheep got away, or exactly when. What is reported is the basic plot. New home, new owner, and apparently a very quick decision that the arrangement was not for the sheep.

Police and animal wranglers have been involved in the search, which suggests the owner is not the only one hoping for a happy ending. So far, the sheep has proven better at hiding than anyone has proven at finding it.

Stories like this are a reminder that moving day is stressful for every species. Animals taken to unfamiliar surroundings can panic and run, and a frightened animal in open country can be difficult to locate and even harder to approach.

For now there is no word on a capture, and no update on the sheep's condition. If anyone in the area spots a wandering woolly runaway, the sensible move is presumably to contact the authorities already working the case rather than freelance a rodeo.
d8f91bd27568.summary: A sheep escaped shortly after arriving at its new owner's Connecticut home and has not been seen in days, police and animal wranglers told UPI. The search continues.
d8f91bd27568.pixel_take: Fastest exit interview on record: the sheep reviewed its new home, gave zero stars, and is now apparently living off the grid. Wool you look at that.
d8f91bd27568.why_it_matters: This is a quirky local story, not a market mover, but it shows how small mishaps can pull in public resources like police time. For anyone buying livestock or pets, secure fencing and a careful arrival plan are cheap compared with the cost of a lost animal.
key_points: A sheep escaped shortly after arriving at its new owner's home in Connecticut.
Police and animal wranglers say it has not been seen in days.
No capture has been reported, per UPI.

5295f5b691da.headline: Weekend Bitcoin Sale Gets a 37.3% Discount, and Thin Markets Are to Blame
body: Bitcoin traded on Kraken's Canadian dollar market at an average 37.3% discount to a benchmark built from the exchange's US dollar trades over a 14-hour stretch, according to Cointelegraph. The gap shows how much the price of a sale can depend on the market where it happens.

The full original article was not available, so the details here come only from the headline and teaser. The headline points to market depth as the driver, meaning how many buy orders are waiting at various prices to absorb a sale.

Here is the general principle. In a deep market, a large sell order meets plenty of buyers close to the current price. In a thin market, the order eats through the available bids and pushes the price lower with each step. That effect is called slippage, and it gets worse when fewer traders are around, as on weekends.

The teaser compares two markets on the same exchange: one in Canadian dollars and one in US dollars. Bitcoin is one asset, but each trading pair has its own order book. A thin book can drift far from the benchmark, and a 37.3% average discount is a big drift.

The practical lesson for anyone selling crypto is that the headline price is not always the price you get. Checking the order book, splitting large orders, and picking the most liquid pair can all matter more than the exact moment you hit the sell button.
5295f5b691da.summary: Over 14 hours, Bitcoin traded on Kraken's Canadian dollar market at an average 37.3% discount to a US dollar-based benchmark, Cointelegraph reports, highlighting how market depth shapes sale prices.
5295f5b691da.pixel_take: Same Bitcoin, same exchange, and a 37.3% markdown. Nobody told the order book it was supposed to be a Black Friday sale.
5295f5b691da.why_it_matters: Liquidity decides what your crypto is really worth when you sell. Thin markets can punish sellers with steep discounts, especially off-hours, so depth matters as much as the quoted price. It is also a reminder that fiat pairs on one exchange can behave very differently.
key_points: Bitcoin averaged a 37.3% discount on Kraken's Canadian dollar market over 14 hours.
The benchmark was based on the exchange's US dollar trades.
Market depth determines how much a sale moves the price.

974bf4b3ad66.headline: Cop31 ends without a keystone climate deal, a first in 17 years
body: The Cop31 climate summit has ended without a keystone agreement, the first time in 17 years that countries have failed to reach one, according to The Guardian. The talks were co-chaired by Turkey and Australia.

The aim was a pact that would have injected urgency into climate action. Instead, delegates leave without the headline deal the process was meant to deliver. The teaser available does not spell out which disputes sank the talks, so the exact reasons remain unclear for now.

The co-chair arrangement, with Turkey and Australia sharing the job, was itself a notable feature of this summit. Whether it shaped the outcome is not stated in the material we have, and we won't guess.

Context helps here. UN climate summits run on consensus, meaning every participating country must sign off on the final text. That makes a headline agreement hard to land: one determined holdout, or a few, can stall the whole thing. A 17-year streak of keystone deals shows how rare a total collapse is.

For governments, businesses and investors, a missing deal means less clarity. Companies planning around clean energy, carbon pricing or green finance look to these summits for signals about where policy is heading. Without a clear one, planning gets murkier, though national policies and existing commitments remain in place.
Expect plenty of finger-pointing and analysis in the coming days. The Guardian is running a live explainer on why the talks fell apart, and more detail should emerge about who blocked what.
974bf4b3ad66.summary: Countries at Cop31 failed to agree a keystone deal for the first time in 17 years. The summit, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, was meant to boost urgency on climate action.
974bf4b3ad66.why_it_matters: Climate summits shape signals on energy policy, carbon pricing and green investment. A failed keystone deal leaves businesses and investors with less clarity on where regulation and funding are heading, which can affect long-term planning and energy-sector valuations.
key_points: Cop31 ended without a keystone agreement, a first in 17 years.
Turkey and Australia co-chaired the talks.
The planned pact was meant to add urgency to climate action.

8dee6718f49b.headline: Rotterdam's Old Harbor Rope Gets a Second Career as a Seat That Rocks
body: A Rotterdam design studio, The New Raw, has turned discarded ship rope from the city's harbor into Buoy, a series of 3D-printed public seats, according to Yanko Design. The seats are a warm orange, close to unglazed pottery, and they rock when you shift your weight.

Discarded ship ropes often end up incinerated or turned into lower-value materials, according to project facilitator In4Art. Here the rope took a longer route. IKM Hendrik Veder collected it in Rotterdam, and Healix cleaned and shredded it in Maastricht, then processed the plastic into pellets.

Back in Rotterdam, The New Raw melted the recycled polypropylene and used a robot to print the seats layer by layer. The series used 45 kilograms (about 99 pounds) of recycled plastic. The batch size set how many seats could be made, and each seat carries an engraved batch and production number.

The color is the rope's own, with no added pigments or coatings. Up close, the printed layers stay visible and curve around the bowl like a thumbprint. The shape resembles a spinning top at rest, with a wide rim over a tapered base, which gives the rocking motion and a nod to harbor buoys.
The reviewer notes a rocking seat is not for everyone, since it can cause nausea and dizziness, and suggests pairing it with a conventional bench.

Buoy is a pilot, not a product line. In4Art says scaling up would need a steadier rope supply, color sorting at the point of collection, and processing that can compete economically with new plastic. A city wanting identical seats would have to plan well ahead, and another port's rope might yield different colors and objects.
8dee6718f49b.summary: Rotterdam studio The New Raw printed rocking public seats from recycled harbor rope using 45 kg of plastic. It's a pilot, and scaling would need steady supply, color sorting and competitive costs.
8dee6718f49b.pixel_take: Retired ship rope finally gets a job where the only thing it has to hold is your weight, and it still can't stop swaying like it's on a dock.
8dee6718f49b.why_it_matters: Recycling waste plastic into higher-value products is a test of whether circular design can compete with cheap virgin plastic. Pilots like this show where the real bottlenecks sit: supply, sorting and cost. Those factors decide whether such products reach cities at scale.
key_points: The New Raw printed Buoy seats from 45 kg of recycled harbor rope plastic.
The orange color comes from the rope itself, with no added pigments.
Scaling needs steady rope supply, color sorting and cost parity with new plastic.

676b4edb8443.headline: Estonian trail camera spots a 'unicorn' deer, and no, it isn't a horse with a dental plan
body: A trail camera on an island in Estonia has recorded video of a roe deer that appears to have a single antler growing from the middle of its forehead, according to UPI. The animal has been nicknamed a "unicorn" online.

The footage shows the deer with what resembles one central horn-like growth, rather than the usual pair of antlers mounted on either side of the head. The material available does not say exactly when the video was captured, who operates the camera, or what caused the unusual look.

Because the details are thin, it is worth being careful about what we can say. The report describes the growth only as something resembling a single antler. Why it looks that way has not been explained in the information we have, so any diagnosis would be guesswork.

What we can say is that trail cameras have become a quiet engine of wildlife discovery. Cheap, motion-triggered and battery-powered, they let researchers, hunters and hobbyists capture animals that would never behave naturally with a human standing nearby. Every so often they catch something that goes viral, and a one-antlered deer is a perfect candidate.

For now, the Estonian unicorn remains a charming oddity: a reminder that nature does not always follow the template, and that a motion sensor in the woods can occasionally out-deliver a fantasy novel.
676b4edb8443.summary: A trail camera on an Estonian island filmed a roe deer with what looks like a single antler on its forehead, earning it the nickname 'unicorn', UPI reports.
676b4edb8443.pixel_take: Finally, a unicorn that's low-maintenance: no glitter, no rainbow, just one antler and a motion sensor that caught it doing deer things.
676b4edb8443.why_it_matters: Cheap trail cameras and viral video show how low-cost technology can turn local wildlife into global attention. It is a small example of how affordable sensors keep producing content and data that used to require expensive expeditions.
key_points: A trail camera on an Estonian island filmed a roe deer with what looks like one antler on its forehead.
The animal has been nicknamed a 'unicorn', according to UPI.
The cause of the unusual growth was not given in the available material.

ad4829ce2daa.headline: Google Maps Shows a Clear Blue Line Where West Bank Checkpoints Stand, Wired Reports
body: Google Maps still fails to show permanent Israeli checkpoints, watchtowers and gates on West Bank roads, according to a Wired investigation published in November 2026. Drivers who see soldiers searching cars on the ground see a clean blue route on the world's most popular navigation app.

The stakes are high for the nearly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank, who face more than 900 movement obstacles, including checkpoints that Wired says can be policed with lethal force. Google has added checkpoint alerts in some places elsewhere, Wired notes, a feature introduced during the Covid crisis. Palestinians have instead turned to homemade tools such as the Road Conditions Telegram channel.

Wired spoke with more than a dozen current and former Google employees. One of them, former product manager Rubén Lozano, joined Maps in 2019 and tracked hyperlocal driving rules, from Barcelona emission zones to toll prices in Australia. He then read a report by the Palestinian digital rights group 7amleh, which described Maps' omissions as systematic rather than technical, and decided to fix the West Bank problem. His managers backed and funded the project.

Colleagues warned him it was hard. Wired reports that employees recalled the backlash when Google began using "Palestine" on a regional site, after which Israel's Knesset questioned a company executive. Lozano pressed ahead anyway. He built a prototype using data from an Egyptian company, which reportedly held coordinates for Palestinian- and Israeli-controlled zones and permanent checkpoint locations, information Israel has never published. He planned alerts and clearer marking of the different zones, but rejected routing users differently by nationality over privacy concerns.

He then hit a wall. Google's user research team said its outside vendors could not source Palestinian drivers and would not look for them. Another source told Wired that vendors worried about worker safety. Lozano fell back on personal contacts. According to Wired, his effort collapsed within about six weeks, after six years of work.

Wired also describes how the map treats the territory: a route to the Palestinian town of Rawabi triggers a border-crossing alert, while a route to the neighboring Ateret settlement shows one seamless drive. Google spokesperson Caroline Bourdeau told Wired the company has faced "challenges acquiring comprehensive and reliable data" in the area. Former employees argue Google has solved far larger mapping problems.
ad4829ce2daa.summary: A Wired investigation says Google Maps omits West Bank checkpoints, and that a former product manager's six-year effort to fix it unraveled in about six weeks. Google cites data challenges.
ad4829ce2daa.why_it_matters: Navigation apps are critical infrastructure, and what they leave out can shape safety and daily life. The story shows how data sourcing, politics and corporate risk calculations decide whose reality a product shows. It also raises reputational and regulatory questions for Google's flagship product.
key_points: Wired says Google Maps shows no permanent West Bank checkpoints despite 900+ movement obstacles.
Ex-product manager Rubén Lozano spent six years on a fix that collapsed in about six weeks.
Google cites difficulty obtaining reliable data; former engineers say the company can solve bigger problems.

88a37079168d.headline: Belgium's Skies Go Quiet as Air Traffic Control Joins Anti-Austerity Strike
body: Nearly all flights in Belgium are set to be cancelled on Monday after air traffic controllers said their staff would join a national strike against government austerity measures, according to Al Jazeera.

Skeyes, the company that runs Belgian air traffic control, said it cannot provide regular services at the country's airports and in its airspace between 7am and 9pm local time. It said expected staffing levels would not allow safe handling of normal traffic, so it must temporarily suspend services. Only emergency and safety-critical flights will continue.

Brussels-Charleroi airport, a major European base for low-cost carrier Ryanair, described the situation as a complete shutdown of all the country's airports for a full day. It called the move a last-minute decision with disastrous consequences. Brussels airport said most departing and arriving flights will have to be cancelled. As the Charleroi statement put it, without air traffic control no flights can take off or land.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which speaks for about 25 carriers, said this would be the 11th strike to hit Belgian airspace in 11 months. That is roughly one a month, which makes a strike start to look less like an event and more like a subscription.

The aviation chaos is part of a wider day of action by Belgian unions against reforms and cost-cutting by the governing coalition. A large demonstration is planned in Brussels, and significant disruption is expected on public transport. Schools, government offices and refuse collection may also be affected.

Meanwhile Prime Minister Bart De Wever has been in long talks with coalition partners on a budget that would save 10 billion euros over the next few years to cut the country's high deficit. Earlier in November he offered his resignation after the coalition failed to agree a deal, but King Philippe rejected it and gave him more time.
88a37079168d.summary: Belgium's air traffic controller Skeyes will suspend regular services on Monday as staff join a national strike against austerity, forcing most flights at the country's airports to be cancelled.
88a37079168d.pixel_take: Eleven strikes in eleven months: Belgian airspace now has a more reliable monthly schedule than some of the flights that use it.
88a37079168d.why_it_matters: Repeated aviation strikes hit airlines, travelers and local business with cancellations and lost revenue. The standoff over a 10 billion euro savings plan also shows how hard it is for European governments to trim deficits without a political and economic price.
key_points: Skeyes will suspend regular air traffic services from 7am to 9pm on Monday, so most flights will be cancelled.
Airline representatives say it is the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months.
The strike protests austerity as the government negotiates a 10 billion euro cost-cutting budget.

9e3cb34cea54.headline: A Deep-Sea Robot Hauled Up Something That Challenges Beliefs About Volcanic Blasts
body: Scientists had long believed that explosive volcanic eruptions could not happen at extreme ocean depths. According to Gizmodo, a robot has now brought up something unexpected from the deep that calls that assumption into question.

The teaser for the report also suggests the research may help explain why Challenger Deep is so deep. That is the name of the famously profound spot in the ocean, and the connection hints that volcanic activity could be tied to how such trenches take shape.

The source material available to us is limited to the headline and teaser, so the specifics remain unclear: what exactly the robot retrieved, where it was collected, who led the work and when the findings were made. We are not going to guess at those details.

What the headline does make clear is the shape of the surprise. The prevailing thinking was that the crushing pressure at great depth would suppress violent, explosive eruptions. A sample that appears to contradict that idea would push researchers to revisit their models of how the seafloor behaves.

It is also a reminder of why robotic explorers matter. Humans cannot easily visit these depths, so uncrewed machines act as our hands and eyes, and every retrieval can overturn a textbook rule. We will update this story if fuller details of the study become available.
9e3cb34cea54.summary: A deep-sea robot reportedly retrieved something that challenges the belief that explosive volcanic blasts can't happen at great depth, and the work may help explain why Challenger Deep is so deep, per Gizmodo.
9e3cb34cea54.pixel_take: Turns out the ocean floor didn't read the rulebook. Scientists said no explosions down there, and the deep replied by sending up a surprise via robot courier.
9e3cb34cea54.why_it_matters: Deep-sea robotics is a growing technology field, and discoveries like this show the payoff from building machines that can work under extreme pressure. Better understanding of seafloor geology also feeds into resource exploration and hazard science, areas where investment and policy decisions follow the research.
key_points: A robot retrieved something unexpected from the deep sea, per Gizmodo.
The find challenges the idea that explosive volcanic blasts can't occur at such depths.
The research may also help explain why Challenger Deep is so deep.
